025b84b0-d00d-5c21-a749-98f3596f9d77.name: Boots
025b84b0-d00d-5c21-a749-98f3596f9d77.description: Men’s leather riding boots. The applications of leather in different colours, with representation of geometric patterns, follow the customs and superstitions of the Hausa. The Hausa possessed, in every community, workshops for producing and dyeing articles of leather, though the most out-standing locations are those of Kano and Sokoto in Nigeria; places producing, since the medieval times, the thinnest skins used in Europe. The skins are those of goat, preferably of the males, and the dye receives the local name of *bagaruwa*. This product is usually processed by women, and it is also used for treating dysentery. The products of the Hausa are distributed, by trade, across wide zones of the Sahel and Subsaharian Africa.
keywords: Leather; trade; bedouins

0268e426-50a7-5898-934e-642eb18157d3.name: Chasuble of the green Persian verstements
0268e426-50a7-5898-934e-642eb18157d3.short_description: The ground fabric of this dalamtic, a silk in wark satin, is single-coloured. The centre and sleeve ends are decorated with a silk fabric from Persia. The manufacture of precious silk fabrics had a long-established tradition in Persia when it experienced its last climax under the Safaviden dynasty (AD 1501-1736). Silk fabrics of high quality showing naturalistic designs with reference to the contemporary miniature painting were typical products of the period.

04c6becd-fdd7-5c20-9596-b48f8a6ce25a.name: Traditional bridal costume and jewellery
04c6becd-fdd7-5c20-9596-b48f8a6ce25a.short_description: This set of traditional clothing gives an overall picture of the universally recognized aesthetics displayed in the festive women’s outfits in Macedonia in the 19th century. Bridal costumes worn in the area of Dolni Polog were distinctive for the great number of varied garments they comprised. The costume, consisting of a *fusta*, a kind of undershirt; a *bunda*, a thicker undergarment; chemise; tunic; vest and other garments, was abundantly decorated with embroidery. It was also richly embellished with jewellery and accessorized with distinctive headdress. Even the headdress included more than one article: a fez made of red baize, a hair band called a *votus* adorned with strings of coins as well as a transparent silk scarf decorated with embroidery, fringes and sequins.

07fa4973-f69d-57f4-8e6d-caeb88f75252.name: Belt with buckles
07fa4973-f69d-57f4-8e6d-caeb88f75252.short_description: Buckles were the most prominent articles of adornment worn by Macedonian women. They were also the most frequently worn pieces of jewellery, having been an inevitable element of folk costumes in all parts of Macedonia. Combining functionality and aesthetics, buckles were also considered to play a protective role. The diverse shapes – round, rectangular, leaf-shaped, etc., as well as the exquisite style of their decorating, show the remarkable skill and talent of goldsmiths producing them. These buckles consist of two slightly concave round plates joined with a little round piece used for fastening. They are adorned with decorative stones and decorated with geometric patterns applied by hammering. The belt is made of cotton fabric decorated with geometric and floral patterns by application of silver and gold-wrapped thread and braids.

08314c51-a88c-51cd-93da-fc641ebafef3.name: Coat (*Anterija*)
08314c51-a88c-51cd-93da-fc641ebafef3.short_description: Starting in the late fifteenth century, modern day Albania belonged to the Ottoman Empire for more than four hundred years. The traditional clothing there is thus very strongly influenced by the Ottomans, as is seen in this floor-length coat. The neck is cut round and the overlong sleeves are slit at the bottom. The garment is fastened in the middle by 41 ornamentally trimmed metal buttons reaching to the waist. Richly ornamental embroidery in appliqué technique cover the coat. The lining consists of a vertically striped *ikat*.

085d1bb8-7770-5c15-929d-7644cdd9063f.name: Headdress.
085d1bb8-7770-5c15-929d-7644cdd9063f.description: The Palestinians of Hebron and the surrounding villages call this type of cap an *araqiyeh*. It is circular with a pointed centre and elaborately embroidered with red and black cross-stitched geometric decoration. Attached to the back of the cap are silver Ottoman coins. The two multicoloured hair-bands (*laffayef*), together with the thin black ribbons fixed to either side of the cap, are modern replacements. This type of headdress has been worn in the Hebron area from the late AH 13th century / AD late 19th century to the present day. During the British mandate in Palestine, the hair-bands (which were used for tying up the hair into a round bun that rested on the back of the neck) were much longer and were made of plaited woollen thread. This headdress was made for everyday use.
085d1bb8-7770-5c15-929d-7644cdd9063f.short_description: The Palestinian women of Hebron and the surrounding villages call this type of headdress an *araqiyeh*. 0b5fcd9e-c601-56fc-a163-574f42dfce20.name: Cape of the Infante Don Felipe.
0b5fcd9e-c601-56fc-a163-574f42dfce20.description: Almost semi-circular cape belonging to the Infante Don Felipe; one of the most representative pieces of the 13th century. Most of it is kept in the National Archaeological Museum. When restored in 1997, the known fragments (I, V, D and J in Madrid and the Cooper Union Museum for the Arts in New York) were added to others kept in the Victoria and Albert Museum in London, the Museums of the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Lyons, the Art Institute of Chicago and the Royal Museums of Art and History in Brussels, as well as a small fragment in the National Archaeological Museum itself (inventory no. 51016). The fabric is made of blue, natural, red and yellow silk with gold thread, woven in taquete and decorated with taffeta-weave stitches on a foundation warp over the crossing of the foundation weave and other wefts, resulting in a matt fabric that appears fully woven with defined edges. The piece is decorated with knotwork with simplified knots, eight-pointed stars, quatrefoils and plant arabesques both on the inside and the intermediate spaces. The edges are finished with ornamental epigraphic bands with the word *baraka*, 'happiness' repeated in *kufic* characters from left to right and vice versa consecutively.
0b5fcd9e-c601-56fc-a163-574f42dfce20.short_description: This silk cape with golden threads and Arabic inscriptions was found in the tomb of the Infante Don Felipe, who chose to be buried wearing it, evidence of the esteem in which the Christian aristocracy held such Andalusian-style fabrics.
0b5fcd9e-c601-56fc-a163-574f42dfce20.dates: 13th century, before 1274, the year in which the Infante died.
0b5fcd9e-c601-56fc-a163-574f42dfce20.method_for_datation: The Infante is known to have died in 1274 and he was buried with the cape.
0b5fcd9e-c601-56fc-a163-574f42dfce20.method_for_provenance: The cape was found in the tomb.
0b5fcd9e-c601-56fc-a163-574f42dfce20.provenance: Tomb of the Templar church of Villalcazar de Sirga, Palencia, Spain.
0b5fcd9e-c601-56fc-a163-574f42dfce20.obtention: The piece was assigned to the National Archaeological Museum as part of the organisation of the Royal Natural History Museum collection in 1867.

0cc82bad-3c43-57b4-a06b-eee73296523f.name: Jana o’ Narr Dress
0cc82bad-3c43-57b4-a06b-eee73296523f.description: Dress with wide sleeves and made of white cotton and silk with red, green, and thin, dark blue stripes. The chest panel has striped Kashmir fabric with wavy edges. The neck and shoulders have additional silk cloth and braid work surrounding the chest panel. The sleeves have silk fabric (“bird’s tongue”) in addition to the original cotton fabric colour. The front and back panels have no embroidery work, and the border is done in wavy needlework. This dress is handmade by the women of Tubas (in the Nablus district) for special occasions and weddings. Traditional Palestinian costumes reflect complex social systems that express the owners’ social status, wealth, region and origins through different designs and decorative elements. In this case, both married and single women can wear this dress, but it is usually worn by the wealthy class of women because the fabric is very expensive and not easy to obtain. Wearing this dress is a visual statement that the owner of the dress is from the upper class of society.

0db9b6f4-876c-52ec-9ce4-b7a1827400e3.name: Coat (*Attila*) for a commander of the Macedonian reform-gendarmerie
0db9b6f4-876c-52ec-9ce4-b7a1827400e3.short_description: According to the agreements at Mürzsteg in 1903 between Austrian Emperor Francis Joseph I and the Tsar of Russian, the international community was sending police officers into the region of Macedonia in order to support and modernize the Macedonian police force. These officers submitted to the orders of the Sultan as the supreme commander of the Imperial Ottoman Army. Against the will of Russia, all international police officers wore a uniform in the Ottoman style: an *attila* like the one seen here. The official headwear was supposed to be the typical local fez, but officers from Austria, Russia and France adopted instead a *Kalpak* made of fur.

0eb45a82-3f02-52db-8222-86625075ccdf.name: Bridal coat (*Klashenik*)
0eb45a82-3f02-52db-8222-86625075ccdf.short_description: A *klashenik* is a kind of over-garment women used to wear in winter. It is split in the front and made of thick woollen broadcloth called *klashna*. This piece is long to the hips. It is adorned with red braids along the hems. It is also decorated with embroidery of geometric patterns on the sleeves and at the breasts. Every ethnic area in Macedonia had distinct style of traditional costume, yet all of them show undeniable influence of Oriental art.

11568132-d5af-54cf-9a3f-f663abfb4f5b.name: Winter jacket
11568132-d5af-54cf-9a3f-f663abfb4f5b.short_description: Sleeveless jacket made of woollen fabric of red and black stripes, decorated with floral motifs of orange and purple colour with couching in silk threads on the shoulders and the bottom. This object illustrates the variegated population composition of the Jordanian territory in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, influenced by the local economy. The main activities were trade and crafts that influenced population movements and the coexistence of various local and foreign communities.

123265a3-960f-5c76-9487-14f718823b74.name: *Termeh* panel
123265a3-960f-5c76-9487-14f718823b74.short_description: Very popular both in the Eastern world and in Europe, ‘Kashmir shawls’ (Pers. *termeh*) were produced not only in northern India but also in Iran, mostly in Kerman. *Termeh* panels, embroidered with metal thread (in the *sermeh duzi* technique) and occasionally with pearls, were treasured family possessions handed down from generation to generation. When used as wedding gifts they included inscriptions of good wishes to the bride and groom. This sumptuous *termeh* panel features scrolling vines and grapes embroidered with silver strips on the wool ground decorated with *botehs*. Various alternating metal strips and a profusion of pearls enhance the highly suggestive tactile quality of this exquisite embroidery.

1313c11f-d35a-5fba-85ac-6b580ca2b754.name: Headdress ornament
1313c11f-d35a-5fba-85ac-6b580ca2b754.short_description: A headdress ornament with the portrait of Fath Ali Shah (1797-1834) in painted enamel. It is shaped as a half-shaped moon combined by the rising sun that was the emblem of the Persian order of honour founded by the Shah in 1807. The bejewelled imperial crown refers to later oil paintings of him, since in the early years of his reign he is usually portrayed in the traditional royal turban topped by an aigrette.

14df710b-1ecd-5f46-9a55-9c8986e98145.name: Fragment of golden lampas with capture scene
14df710b-1ecd-5f46-9a55-9c8986e98145.short_description:
Silk figured fabrics (patterns of which included images of people) were at the peak of the Safavid court fashion. A remarkable example of the type is this fragment of a golden lampas depicting a scene of captivity. One of the most technologically sophisticated and costly fabrics in Iran, the golden lampas provided up to 10 silk threads of different colours in the pattern. The inclusion of threads wrapped in gold or silver foil suggest that the fabric could be produced in *karkhane* – imperial workshops.  
The fragment is one of the two largest pieces among seven dispersed parts of a very costly man’s robe that probably belonged to some member of the Iranian Shah family. The scene featured on the lampas has long aroused great interest among researchers. Around a tree (sycamore or maple), where a large fairy bird is sitting on the branch, rides a horseman leading a prisoner. A little child sits behind the rider. Above the people a rooster flies towards a tree.  
The horseman is depicted in the characteristic Safavid outfit of the AD 16th century: a turban is wound around a tall Taj cap, the number of turban bangs symbolizes 12 righteous Shi‘ite imams.  
The idea to treat the scene as a political manifesto of the victorious campaigns of Shah Tahmasp I to Georgia (1540, 1553) was complemented by alternative *Sufi* interpretation of the subject. The scene of captivity was seen as an allegory of man on his spiritual path to God. Thus the horseman stands for the Teacher who leads the Disciple (captive) through the complex ways of learning towards a divine truth personified by the mythical ancient Iranian bird, Simurg (fairy bird).

15610349-3f4b-5d20-bbb1-76ff1816ce04.name: Kaftan
15610349-3f4b-5d20-bbb1-76ff1816ce04.short_description: Originally worn by a prince or a boyar, the present kaftan was turned at some point into an ecclesiastical cope and preserved as such at the Cozia Monastery (in southwestern Romania), where it was discovered in 1864. By the mid-1950s it was transferred to the Museum, and was later reconstituted into its original form. The long, loose garment with long sleeves is lavishly decorated with eight-petalled rosettes set against a red ground. Each rosette encircles a lotus flower. In between rosettes, a design of delicate scrolls with tiny wild roses.

19c733fc-08e0-52fa-a832-d08a38cebc5d.name: *Tiraz* textile fragment from an *ikat* shawl
19c733fc-08e0-52fa-a832-d08a38cebc5d.short_description: Striped textiles from Yemen were famous in medieval times throughout the Islamic world. They were made in the *ikat* technique, in which cotton warp threads were bundled together and resist-dyed before being arranged on the loom to form striped lozenge patterns. The regularity of the weave and the fineness of the cotton threads of this *tiraz* attest to its status as a luxury object. The gilded inscription in a highly stylised floriated and interlaced *kufic* script includes the line “Dominion belongs to Him \[God\].”
19c733fc-08e0-52fa-a832-d08a38cebc5d.dates: Hegira second half 3rd–early 4th century / AD late 9th–early 10th century

1b9107ef-851d-52ee-bc3e-ab6407fccbb8.name: Sarong
1b9107ef-851d-52ee-bc3e-ab6407fccbb8.short_description:
The harmonious marriage of the iridescent colours in Malay textiles is perhaps best seen in examples of finely woven *kain limar*. The single weft-ikat cloth, also known as *kain lemar* or *kain limau*, is principally produced in the state of Terengganu and Kelantan on the East Coast of the Malay Peninsula. While these cloths are now associated with the Sultanate of Terengganu, in the past they were also part of royal ceremonial costume in the Riau and Lingga archipelago, which lie between the Malay Peninsula and southern Sumatra.

1c5f02d2-2470-50be-8d9d-69e9381c662f.name: Clogs
1c5f02d2-2470-50be-8d9d-69e9381c662f.description:
*Nanule* – clogs (Tr. *nalın*) are a major category of Ottoman footwear, worn both by men and women. They were carved from a single piece of hardwood, such as walnut, beech, boxwood or ash, held on the foot by a leather strap and usually decorated with mother-of-pearl inlay or metal plaques. The wooden soles of the clogs have two high wedges, as they were designed for use on wet floors in the hamam – a Turkish bath. The height of the clogs also protected the foot from the heat generated by underfloor heating in the bath.  
  
These clogs, from the Museum of Applied Art in Belgrade (a.n. TC-265 (1924), are made of wood. They have flared wedges, the back one expanded at the rear. The toe of the sole is square, and the heel is pointed. The soles and wedges are inlaid with mother-of-pearl and metal wire. The inlay design features mother-of-pearl triangles set within metal wire frames. The leather straps are covered with purple velvet and embroidered with vegetable motifs in couched supported technique, using metal thread and spangles. The clogs had an important place in the shared dress and living culture of the urban population in the Ottoman Balkans, which had diverse confessional and ethnic backgrounds.
1c5f02d2-2470-50be-8d9d-69e9381c662f.method_for_datation: By stylistic and comparative analysis with related material.
1c5f02d2-2470-50be-8d9d-69e9381c662f.obtention: The item is a part of the collection of Serbian painter and engraver Ljuba Ivanović (1882–1945). The collection was purchased by the Museum of Applied Art in Belgrade in 1951 and comprises 3,116 items, bearing witness to the early modern and modern visual culture of the Balkans: urban and folk dress,  jewelry, metalwork, casting molds and tools, items carved in wood, horn, and mother-of-pearl, wood-carved and painted icons, etc. The items were collected in the field, mostly during the interwar period.

1cd784d6-18b3-56c5-be73-779aee36490e.name: Widow’s Dress from Bir al-Sabe
1cd784d6-18b3-56c5-be73-779aee36490e.description: A dress for widowed women only, from Bir al-Sabe. This dress displays heavy embroidery work on the chest panel, similar to a *qalayed* (necklace) motif. The embroidery of this dress is less festive and detailed and adorned with few birds or flower motifs. The neck and shoulders are embroidered on each side and display orange *hirmizi* needlework with few flower shapes. The sleeves show varied embroidery designs, while the *banayeq* (side panels) and the front and back panels show heavy embroidery work in blue with cypress tree and feather motifs, along with talismans on the top of the side panels. This dress has a very unusual and interesting feature; at the bottom of the dress (*dyara*) there is thick blue embroidery, but the dress is devoid of embroidery in the middle. This design feature holds deep social meaning, denoting that the owner of the dress is a widowed, unmarried woman who does not intend to marry again. On the other hand, if the woman fills the gap in the middle with embroidery, this added embellishment is a declaration of her intention to marry again.

1f0eaf20-2956-56be-9d41-aa6ed59baf58.name: Robe for a man or a child
1f0eaf20-2956-56be-9d41-aa6ed59baf58.short_description:
The outside of the upper garment (*gaba*) is made of a purple silk changeant, whilst its cuffs are lined on the inside with a Persian wool fabric with a characteristic striped pattern. Since the cuffs are usually turned inside out, this creates a pleasant colour contrast. European printed fabric was used to make the lining, as was often the case during the latter 19th century.  
  
The *gaba* is a traditional outer garment whose shape has changed little over the centuries. The upper part is close-fitting, while the lower part is flared and sometimes has side slits.  
  
This robe was acquired by the Swiss merchant Emil Alpiger in Iran between 1870 and 1896. Alpiger was then director of the Manchester-based trading company Ziegler & Co. which owned a carpet factory in Sultanabad.

2065193b-8c2b-5f0c-9ce1-122837e27dc7.name: Woman’s robe (*entari*)
2065193b-8c2b-5f0c-9ce1-122837e27dc7.short_description: Traditional Ottoman clothing was designed to conceal the figure, which explains the use of several superimposed garments. On the other hand, these multiple layers emphasized the great variety of fabrics, the striking colour contrasts, and the rich texture of the embroidered pieces. The *entari* is typical for the Ottoman female dress: ankle-length or shorter, generally open down the front, it has long, narrow sleeves slit at the elbow to reveal the embroidered areas, as well as the colours and decoration on the sleeves of the garment underneath. Dense silk embroidery covers the entire surface of this *entari*. The floral patterns and the architectural details are stylistically similar to the rich decoration on certain embroideries of daily use dating from the same period.

21d264d1-3d1b-5ec6-b7d4-e5b54eaaed68.name: *Bindallı entari*
21d264d1-3d1b-5ec6-b7d4-e5b54eaaed68.short_description: The attire of Ottoman women included dresses for the outdoors and the indoors. Starting from early 19th century, dresses called *üçetek* (dress with three skirts) and *dörtetek* (dress with four skirts) became fashionable. As relations with Europe increased, women in Istanbul started to use imported European textiles for their new dresses. This *entari* (dress) is made of purple velvet embroidered in the *bindallı* (dress that has embroidered flowers on the branches) style with garlands and flowers in vases in the *dival* (gold or silver embroidery on velvet) technique using silver-gilt thread. It has a short front opening, round neck and fitted sleeves. The skirt is widened by triangular gores and is longer at the back.

22b59916-1001-5666-873e-2d7a62f3d991.name: *Keswa kabbous (wedding outfit)*
22b59916-1001-5666-873e-2d7a62f3d991.short_description: Worn by the bride during the wedding ceremony, the keswa kabous el-Jaraq weighs more than ten kilograms. It consists of a large, billowing pair of trousers secured at the waist by a tekka (similar to a ribbon), with a matching top, short enough to leave the waist uncovered, both made of silk taffeta. Its air of great wealth and elegance comes particularly from the contrast between the floral motifs, embroidered with a flat silver thread, and the sequins, also sewn on with a gold and silver thread. When worn by a seated bride, the trousers resemble a large hoop-skirt, connected to a low-necked bodice, which together give the impression of being a robe de cour (grand habit). The upper section of these trousers, hemmed at the waist but open at the front, consists of almost four metres of fabric, and the legs alone have a circumference of one and a half metres and are a metre long. The end of the legs is hemmed with some robust percale fabric, which contains the hemming and rises up the leg to create an even larger swell around the ankle.

2363b57a-3e83-58d6-add7-b8e17a845595.name: Belt elements
2363b57a-3e83-58d6-add7-b8e17a845595.short_description: Composed of a central rosette, eight bars and two finials, these belt elements are decorated with domes and granulation designs. Several features compare with Iranian pieces including the box construction and the minute granulation covering completely most of the domes. An early date is supported by the conspicuous absence of openwork filigree used in Fatimid jewellery. Similar belt elements were found in the Bekaa valley in Lebanon, in a hoard of Mamluk and other later jewellery.

2648874b-264b-5142-94b8-f20ea33a01b4.description: Historical fans were popular accessories in the second half of the 19th century, especially those commemorating important public events such as North Africans wars. These everyday objects as fans would serve as tools to disseminate political or social ideas. The employment of lithography applied to the leaf tells us of the propaganda use of the engraving and its application to the decorative arts. This fan is an example of it, because it shows the Spanish army helping the people from the villages in Spanish territory of North Africa (Morocco).

26bb48d2-0468-5e95-b709-f3f74817bef6.name: Man's trousers (*Chakshiri*)
26bb48d2-0468-5e95-b709-f3f74817bef6.short_description: There used to be around fifty diverse styles of folk costumes worn in different ethnic areas throughout Macedonia in the 19th century and in the early 20th century. Among the most prominent were the costumes of Gorni Polog. Unlike the diverse and numerous women’s garments, men’s outfits were much simpler and rather unified. These men's trousers of white canvas are decorated plainly with black braids.

274e910c-7ec1-5f20-8460-292341da7d08.name: Headdress
274e910c-7ec1-5f20-8460-292341da7d08.short_description: Three silver chains formed into a hat with beaded frontispiece decorated with coins. On the back, a long fabric with gold and silver Ottoman and Venice coins. Silver jewellery was the most common, because only rich people could afford gold jewellery. The dowry of silver and gold jewellery was given by the groom to the bride, reflecting the financial status of the groom. The Jordanian economy relied on trades and crafts and new waves of people started to come to Jordan and began to settle for these purposes. This object is an example of how traditional fashion reflected the variegated population composition of Jordan in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It is also an example of local personal attire, fashion, costumes and rites.

279e1f50-df40-5f44-a5e0-e9a46ddf29b7.name: Bridal coat (*Klashenik*)
279e1f50-df40-5f44-a5e0-e9a46ddf29b7.short_description: A *klashenik* is a kind of over-garment in varying lengths and split on the front made of thick woollen broadcloth called *klashna*. This knee-length piece comes from the Veles Region. It is abundantly adorned with embroidery above the lower hem and at the breasts. Embroidery was an inevitable part of decorating the majority of Macedonian folk costumes. The exquisite, meticulously executed embroidery applied on this tunic makes it a real work of art.

29f9716b-3b17-5ea5-b1e6-06de5e5b0e3e.name: *Funda* (pin)
29f9716b-3b17-5ea5-b1e6-06de5e5b0e3e.short_description: Over the course of the centuries-long existence of Macedonia in the shadow of the Ottoman Empire there was apparent reflection of Oriental-Islamic influences in its arts and crafts. This also applies to the jewellery of Macedonians and all other ethnic communities. In the east of Macedonia, young women and brides within the Vlach population used to wear exquisite articles of adornment in the area of the temples. This type of jewellery was called *funda*. It was usually in trapezoid or semi-oval shape. *Funda* was made in filigree technique richly adorned with lace and tiny silver coins.

2a7ae5f9-624f-523e-9ba6-163799cfc234.name: Silk lampas robe
2a7ae5f9-624f-523e-9ba6-163799cfc234.short_description:
This monumental silk lampas robe from Sogdiana, carbon dated to the seventh to eighth century, has raised theories regarding its role and function. In religious context, this silk fabric was known to wrap religious text or relics, and bodies for burial purposes. In diplomatic relation, the weft fabric functioned as diplomatic gifts, or tailored into costumes for government officials. This silk robe presents us an image of the luxurious textiles traded between China, Central Asia and Persia.  
The Sassanians used to weave their own designs on silk - elaborate repeating motifs of heraldic animal and human elements with interlocking plant enclosed within a pearl-like roundel - which achieved popularity in Central Asia. The Sogdians are known to weave motifs specific to their target market by appealing to ethnic and culture, religious purposes or the ruling elite. By the eighth century, Sassanian motifs were brought into being as both imported goods and locally-produced reproduction especially from Sogdiana.
2a7ae5f9-624f-523e-9ba6-163799cfc234.bibliography: Watt, J. C. Y., *When Silk Was Gold : Central Asian and Chinese Textiles*, New York: Metropolitan Museum of Art in cooperation with the Cleveland Museum of Art, 1997. Kadoi, Y., *Islamic Chinoiserie: the Art of Mongol Iran*, Edinburgh: Edinburgh University Press, 2009. Rees, B.R., Jervis, M.E., *Lampas: a new approach to Greek*, Oxford: Blackwell, 1970.
materials: Stitched and woven with fine red, green, blue and cream silk threads

2d85c81f-8fff-5170-9719-df9f41dbd763.name: Socks (*Chorapi*)
2d85c81f-8fff-5170-9719-df9f41dbd763.short_description: In the 18th, 19th and early 20th centuries, all garments for the entire family were made by women themselves. They used to weave all the fabrics, except for the broadcloth, as well as to cut and sew the clothes, decorate them by embroidery and apply varied ornaments for embellishing. Women also used to knit the socks to match the outfit. These men’s socks belong to the set of traditional men’s costume from the Gorni Polog area. They are knitted from black wool and *srma* (silver and gold-wrapped threads). They have been additionally decorated with embroidered floral patterns in different colours.

2f8b920a-ec65-5c26-a6f7-a26f55c2895e.name: Kaftan fragment.
2f8b920a-ec65-5c26-a6f7-a26f55c2895e.description:
A silk brocade (*kemha*) fragment that originally formed the back of a child’s collarless, short-sleeved kaftan, cut with a straight waist and bell-shaped skirt. The textile is woven with a dense, overall design of eight-pointed stars set in staggered rows on a crimson ground.  
The original museum record states that this piece represents a portion of a child's robe-of-honour from Constantinople or Bursa. Possibly arriving in Turkey via Syria, the complex weaving technique adopted on this textile, known as lampas weave, was used by Ottoman weavers in the late AH 9th–early 10th /AD late 15th–early 16th century. The most important Ottoman silk manufactory was at Bursa but in the AH 10th / AD 16th century, court workshops were also set up in Istanbul, the Ottoman capital. *Kemha* garments were designed to emphasise the imperial status of the sultan and his family even in death, when such garments were often draped over imperial cenotaphs or *sanduka*s.  
This fragment is part of a group of garments that was brought to Europe by an art dealer and cut up with some of the resulting front and back sections subsequently divided between the V&A in London and the Royal Museum in Edinburgh.
2f8b920a-ec65-5c26-a6f7-a26f55c2895e.short_description: Royal child kaftans were among the products made in the Imperial Ottoman silk weaving centres at Bursa and Istanbul. The so-called *kemha* costumes were designed to emphasise the imperial status of members of the court, even in death when such garments were often draped over imperial cenotaphs or *sandukas*.
2f8b920a-ec65-5c26-a6f7-a26f55c2895e.dates: Hegira, late 10th–early 11th century / AD late 16th– early 17th century.
2f8b920a-ec65-5c26-a6f7-a26f55c2895e.method_for_datation: *Kemha* textiles were popular in the Ottoman Empire between the late 10th–early 11th / late 16th–early 17th centuries.

30f8c92a-d056-538d-835c-8f96181283c0.description: This *malaq* dress originates in the Al-Khadir area of Bethlehem District, where women embroider it by hand. It is worn only by brides for their wedding day. This dress is made with *Abu Warda* fabric. It has a traditional *malaq* chest panel of flower pot motifs, bordered by two pieces of blue velvet fabric with a bird embroidered on them. The neck and shoulders are made of red fabric. The sleeves are made with silk *hirmizi* cloth in addition to the original fabric of the dress and are embroidered with a Bethlehem clock and a bird. The *banayeq* (side panels) are embroidered with clock and floral motifs in addition to multiple crosses. Traditional Palestinian costumes are characterized by strong emphasis on decoration and colour and are designed from the finest and most expensive fabrics, as shown by this dress.

324db717-f88f-51eb-8d77-e05946d136f3.name: Headdress ornament.
324db717-f88f-51eb-8d77-e05946d136f3.description:
Made up of a nickel silver-plate disc with metal chains, Ottoman coins, charms and beads, this headdress ornament would have been worn as part of a bridal outfit, fixed to the top of a bonnet made of embroidered fabric, and shaped to fit the head. One of the charms is a French medal of Saint Joseph, and the other is the Hand of Fatima. The coins, except for one Spanish coin that shows the name of King Phillip V of Spain, are Ottoman, dated between AH 1180 and 1260 (AD 1766–1844). The coins in such headdresses had two functions, one simply about decoration, and the other as an indicator of the bride's wealth; her social status and the value of her dowry. The presence of the Christian saint's medal centred in the front section of the disk draws attention to the probability that this headdress may have belonged to a Christian bride! In Palestine, which is full of intermingling Christian and Muslim villages, this headdress is a good example of the cultural diversity of the Ottoman Middle East. Other European coins popular in Middle Eastern jewellery include coins depicting the Austrian Empress Maria Theresa.  
  
The brides of Ramallah (a predominantly Christian town) would have worn headdresses such as this one for their wedding celebrations. A woman would be free to either add more coins or to take some off for personal use, for home improvements for example. Many of these headdresses were passed down through generations, and when gold coins came into fashion, many of the silver coins were replaced.
324db717-f88f-51eb-8d77-e05946d136f3.short_description: A Christian saint’s medal attached to the front of this ornament reveals that it belonged to an Arab Christian bride from the Ottoman period in Palestine. It would have been worn as part of the bridal outfit of a lady from Ramallah. The silver coins are Ottoman from between AH 1180 and 1260 (AD 1766–1844).

3385951b-c80c-5d8e-8659-f32b8e5ee6a7.short_description: Analysis of the evolution path of traditional costumes in the Republic of Macedonia have shown apparent influences of the Old Slav, Old Balkan, Byzantine and Turkish-Oriental cultures. This piece of traditional overcoat is an exquisite example of the application of *srma* – gold and silver-wrapped thread used widely in the Oriental handicraft of decorating garments. A *gornik* is a sleeveless upper garment made of white broadcloth called *klashna*. It has false sleeves hanging on the back. They are actually strips of white broadcloth richly adorned with pompoms of fluffy red wool, silver thread braids, a silver twisted ribbon, red baize, a silver string, sequins and beads. The lower part of the back is decorated in the same manner. Its rims and seams are also decorated with red and black braids.

3a2530bf-22b3-5651-bacc-f8a748c678a1.short_description: A rectangular piece of cotton cloth embroidered with cross-stitching forming a bonnet with a line of 70 gold coins (*ghawasi*) sewn together on the front, with two pieces of cloth on the top sides with silver Ottoman coins and red stuffed velvet pursed from the back side with 7 silver Ottoman coins. It illustrates common elements and traditions in the area in fashion, costumes and social rites. There were no political boundaries at that period between the Jordanian and Palestinians territories. Some cities were like twins because of their close proximity and the exchange of trade goods and business.

3a71d542-5e72-54c9-808c-51df8069dd8b.name: Ikhdari Dress (*Malaq*)
3a71d542-5e72-54c9-808c-51df8069dd8b.description: *Malaq* dress made of *Abu Warda* fabric and *Ikhdari* fabric with green, burgundy, orange and black stripes. The dress has a chest panel embroidered with the image of a vase (the traditional chest panel of a *malaq* garment) and is adorned with two pieces of blue velvet embroidered with a bird. The sleeves are wide, made of *Hormozi* silk fabric, with an *Al-Talhami* clock shape and embellished with a bird motif. Embroidery on the chest panel resembles the traditional stitch of *malaq* dress with floral motifs, while the collar on the neck and shoulders is made with pink cloth and connected to the chest panel by a line of russet velveteen trim. The front of the dress shows the original fabric colors without embroidery, while the back panel shows four horizontal stripes of the fabric. The *banayeq* (side panels) are of silk cloth and are connected to the dress by *manajel* (thick braid work connecting the dress parts). The bottom sections of the *banayeq* are adorned with simple floral motif embroidery and some crosses. This dress is worn by women for weddings and other special occasions.

418d5f13-426c-5a27-b41a-2628f935f8f4.name: Talismanic Shirt
418d5f13-426c-5a27-b41a-2628f935f8f4.short_description:
A rich display of calligraphy covers this garment belonging to a group of magic objects called Islamic Talismanic shirts. Sewn from cream-colored cotton, the caftan is adorned with blue and red ink as well as liquidized gold.  
  
The Qur’an refers to Prophet Yusuf wearing a similar protective shirt, written to have restored sight in Yusuf’s father, Yacub. In Turkey, sultans would gear up with this robe for battles as spiritual and bulletproof armour.  
  
This example from 17th century Turkey shimmers with Qur’anic verses in *naskh* and *ruqqa* calligraphy. The verses include the *Surat al-Fatiha* (opening chapter of the Qur’an), *Ayat al-Kursi* (the Throne Verse), the *Surat Yasin* against evil sorcery, and the verse “Help from God and a speedy victory” from Surat al-Saff. The squares emphasize Mohammed and Allah in *kufic* script. Prayers enrich the magical shirt in bilateral symmetry. Furthermore, the first four caliphs and ninety-nine beautiful names of God appear within the fabric. Additional amuletic signs hide in plain sight, obscured in magical shapes and the science of letters (*ilm al huruf*). As one of the most efficacious inscriptions, the beautiful names of God may each represent a letter, planet, a day and an angel.  
  
Predominantly from India, Iran and Turkey between the 14th and 17th centuries, the wearer embodies the caftan’s healing power. The textile functions as a vehicle for the interaction of the body and sacred script, simultaneously blessing and protecting the person reading, touching or wearing the jacket. When gifted, the talismanic shirt amplifies the connection between the gift-giver and recipient.

482b2fe7-2ab8-521c-aeb6-542db13d4285.name: Chasuble
482b2fe7-2ab8-521c-aeb6-542db13d4285.description:
The background is made of red silk velvet embroidered with different silver threads. The white silver stitches blocking the metallic threads create many different surface motifs of different heights, and flat areas thanks to a light padding.  
Most likely manufactured in Bologna, this vestment has a common decorative scheme especially evident in the chasuble. It is divided in three by a central rich bush of acanthus interlaced with the instruments of the Passion of Christ forming the main decorative feature. Great inflorescences alternate with the crown of thorns, the cock and the glove. They build a sort of central axis from which depart wide branches linked by delicate nets and vine shoots. The vestment is clearly indebted to models made in Rome in the age of Pope Benedict XIV, such as the ones donated to the Cathedral of San Pietro in Bologna. This is evident in the use of the silver thread as a reflective surface. The ample motif extended on a flat surface and the symmetrical disposition of the main shoots lead to Emilian decorative schemes and patterns. The colour red of the vestment and the symbols of the Passion might suggest a use connected with the feast of the Exaltation of the Cross or the Invention of the Cross, the sacrifice of Christ might also be generally referred to martyrdom.  
The high quality of the work was recognized in 1900 when the vestment was sent to the exhibition of sacred art held in Bologna, in the church of San Francesco. In 1926 this same vestment was photographed by the local Soprintendenza in one of the first campaigns documenting church heritage.
482b2fe7-2ab8-521c-aeb6-542db13d4285.short_description: The red background of the chasuble is divided by silver lace in fields. Two leaf garlands curl against a net ground; the sides are marked with a garland pattern in front of a net ground. The central pole springs from an acanthus bush holding the instruments of the Passion of Christ in its spires. Veil, burse, stole and maniple are embroidered using the most decorative patterns from the design.

49567841-9478-56f0-9dd2-ff37377f69f1.name: Womanʼs jacket
49567841-9478-56f0-9dd2-ff37377f69f1.short_description:
After 1873, Iranian women of the upper classes wore a short skirt imitating the French *tutu* worn by ballet dancers. Called *shalitah*, this little skirt was combined with a small jacket, kept above the waist so as not to spoil the puffy effect of the *shalitah*, with long sleeves worn over a thin shirt.  
  
As was customary at the time, the outer fabric is a Persian *qalamkar*, a printed fabric that is intricately handmade, whist in contrast, cheap European printed cotton fabrics was used, as was convention, for the lining. However, the two fabrics were not combined at random, and it is clear from the intriguing contrast that much attention was given to the choice of these two patterns. In this particular case, the contrast between the lively, handmade pattern and its machine-made counterpart is especially striking.  
  
This jacket was acquired by the Swiss merchant Emil Alpiger in Iran between 1870 and 1896. Alpiger was then director of the Manchester-based trading company Ziegler & Co. which owned a carpet factory in Sultanabad.

4b1cc99c-bdcc-51e9-bf03-770c80101277.short_description: There used to be around fifty diverse styles of folk costumes worn in different ethnic areas throughout Macedonia in the 19th century and in the early 20th century. Among the most prominent were the costumes of Gorni Polog. Unlike the diverse and numerous women’s garments, men’s outfits were much simpler and rather unified. This upper garment called a *mintan* is of plain cut. It is made of silk in a striped pattern. Its only decorations are pieces of black cloth applied to the sleeves.

4b852956-5f21-5509-913e-4ba87cf57f09.name: Gilet
4b852956-5f21-5509-913e-4ba87cf57f09.short_description:
Golden embroidery graces the Ottoman vest in floral and circle arrangements resembling lotus buds. The glossy threads and red gemstones highlight the elegance of the cream-colored silk called *yelek*.  
  
Across centuries, the traditional costumes remain unisex. This jacket may be worn by children as an inner vest or an overcoat with layers of elaborate garments meeting the requirements of Muslim modesty and the desire for luxury.  
  
While Ottomans adopted shorter jackets from Europe, Turkish attire entered Western fashion in the 19th century. Pieces like this *yelek* appeared at masquerade balls in Britain and became widespread in fashion magazines as trendy clothing restricted to women’s wear. Their influence still permeates today’s runways.

This Turkish and colourful beadwork one, with its traditional geometric pattern and the promise of a fashionable outfit, would have surely delighted any lady.

522f2144-3034-5e4d-9bc3-6ef8c6f5ecd0.name: Veil
522f2144-3034-5e4d-9bc3-6ef8c6f5ecd0.short_description: Three natural cotton and linen fabrics sewn and decorated with cross-stitch with embroidered folkloric patterns (known as “cypress trees”, “amulets”, “keys”, “saw” and “Shuayb teeth”). They are mainly in red with some green colour; a small linen fringe dangles from two sides. The veil was an essential piece of women’s dress. Girls started preparing their trousseau (clothes, shawls, and other belongings collected for marriage) at the age of ten. Married women had various embroidered costumes worn for special occasions. As the economy of the Jordanian territory in the late 19th century-early 20th century relied on trades and crafts, new waves of traders and artisans started to arrive and to settle. Thus, traditional costumes reflect a variegated population composition, demographic changes, personal attire and local rites.

523bb921-1fd6-50c1-866d-04687585ebaa.name: Headscarf
523bb921-1fd6-50c1-866d-04687585ebaa.short_description:
High quality silk fabrics from Tunisia woven with inwoven silver  
and goldthreads were already admired at the London World’s Fair in 1851. In Tunisia, these girdles, sashes, head-cloths or shawls were reserved for the well-to-do. Specialists, organised into guilds since the Middle Ages, dye and weave the imported raw silk. After 1900, the wholesale import of cheap, industrially produced textiles drove the Tunisian silk production out of the market.

531f2f47-2ae4-509e-a2e9-99d2a1ea93da.name: Ornament from a Janissary’s cap
531f2f47-2ae4-509e-a2e9-99d2a1ea93da.short_description: The military supremacy that had helped make the Ottomans a world power was largely based on the highly disciplined Janissary corps – crack infantry troops. As a part of their uniform, the Janissaries wore a distinctive felt hat somewhat like a stocking cap in appearance, known as a *börk*, to which was affixed just above the forehead an ornament such as this rare silver gilt example. The slightly concave device, decorated with delicately worked geometric designs, would have held an insignia demonstrating the Janissary's loyalty to the Sultan–possibly a feather or even a spoon, signifying that it was the ruler who provided him with his daily soup.
531f2f47-2ae4-509e-a2e9-99d2a1ea93da.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
531f2f47-2ae4-509e-a2e9-99d2a1ea93da.method_for_datation: The decoration of this object, including eight- and six-pointed stars against a scrolling background, is identical to janissary hat ornaments captured from the Ottomans after the Battle of Vienna in 1683, establishing a probable terminus ante quem (e.g., Museum of Karlsruhe, Baden Germany).
531f2f47-2ae4-509e-a2e9-99d2a1ea93da.method_for_provenance: The same type of ornament is represented attached to the distinctive Ottoman military hat in paintings, lithographs and photographs of Ottoman janissaries; the hat with ornament carved in stone forms the upper part of janissary tombstones, while a few actual hats have survived with their ornaments (e.g., Museum of Karlsruhe, Baden, Germany).

54310c6d-87ca-585e-b552-bcb1c5951fe3.name: Dress
54310c6d-87ca-585e-b552-bcb1c5951fe3.short_description: This dress of al-Druze (Druse) women is made of a long grey with green and silver brocade, pursed narrow sleeves, wide, open square shaped chest, pursed at the middle and wide at the bottom with ruffles and a cotton liner. This object illustrates the variegated social composition and demographic changes in the Jordanian territory in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The al-Druze tribes migrated from Syria (Hawran) to north east Jordan in the early twentieth century because of their support for the Syrian revolution against the French occupation. The traditional Druse and other Jordanian costumes were influenced by the local trade and economic activities: as illustrated in this case, they were often made of silk textiles, produced in Syria and traded to Jordan and Palestine.

557a3c2b-e69e-533d-a2c9-d263db2c8d12.name: Woman's *entari*
557a3c2b-e69e-533d-a2c9-d263db2c8d12.short_description: *Entari*s were worn over thin silk shifts and baggy *shalvar* trousers and were held at the waist by a sash or belt. They could be worn open or buttoned above the waist. Several *entari*s, made of different fabrics, usually with contrasting colours, were often layered on top of one another. They were more often than not made of luxurious silk striped or brocaded fabrics and trimmed with fine braid or *oya* needlework.

56bae231-ad09-5568-8e83-1f1aa7115444.name: Buckles (*Pafti*)
56bae231-ad09-5568-8e83-1f1aa7115444.short_description: Buckles were distinctive articles of adornment used throughout the centuries by Macedonian women. They were the most frequently worn and most exquisite articles of adornment in Macedonian women’s folk attire. Buckles used to be adorned with stylized geometric and floral patterns, the artistic effect having been emphasized by the application of decorative stones, filigree ornaments, gold-plating, pearls, mother-of-pearl, corals, chains and other embellishments. This outstanding set of buckles in leaf shapes is decorated with pearls and semi-precious stones, by application of the technique of "live" gold-plating.

5714f381-6e11-56d5-9801-fef85803c128.name: Wedding dress
5714f381-6e11-56d5-9801-fef85803c128.short_description: Long black dress, wide at the bottom with narrow sleeves, rounded neck and open chest. Silk linen appliqué, hand embroidery with cross-stitch on the sides, back panel, chest, and sleeves with embroidered folkloric patterns. On the chest: necklace, cypress tree. Side: ivy, amulets, “feathers”. Front: small cypress tree on silk. Back: ivy, cypress tree, pillows, pasha tents. Sleeve: ivy, feather, triangle (amulets). Palestinian women's costumes varied according to each Palestinian city and geographical area. Costumes in the mountain regions were different from those of coastal and desert areas, and had a distinguished embroidery. This costume represents village style. Girls started preparing their trousseau (clothes, shawls and other belongings they collected for their marriage) at the age of ten. Married women's costumes were heavily embroidered. Palestinian weavers used traditional spinning processes using manual spindles to prepare the cotton and linen threads imported from Egypt. Ashkelon city weavers used light vertical hand looms (*Majdalawi* looms) to produce linen fabrics, while silk fabrics were spindled and woven in Syria.

58b8041e-0838-56a2-b0b3-2369a498e868.name: Belt.
58b8041e-0838-56a2-b0b3-2369a498e868.description:
This type of long brocade silk belt, or *lampas*, woven on a draw-loom in the workshops of Fez, appeared in the early AH 12th / AD 18th century. Worn on top of a kaftan by aristocratic and middle-class women, it was wrapped several times around the waist. Folded in half, it could be used on either side. This piece is narrow and flexible like the older examples. On a red background, brocade decoration consisting of five differently coloured motifs inspired by the decorative Moroccan-Andalusian repertoire of is embellished with elements borrowed from Persian and Ottoman art: geometric knotwork whose interstices are decorated with flowers, fleurons and palms, ovoid motifs reminiscent of the fruit of the citrus tree *tronjia*, and friezes of arcades decorated with flowers similar to the designs found on wall hangings. These motifs appear on their own or combined in repetitive alternating transverse bands.  
The two ends of the belt are decorated with several stylised hands and eight-pointed stars, or Solomon's seals, considered in esoteric Moroccan tradition to be prophylactic symbols. Between the large motifs that make up the main decoration of the fabric and the two ends of the belt, a narrow band decorated with small tulips arranged head-to-foot is the mark of the workshop.  
The long cords that finish the belt are knotted at the front to keep it around the waist.
58b8041e-0838-56a2-b0b3-2369a498e868.short_description: This sort of long silk-brocade belt would have been worn above a kaftan by the wives of important dignitaries and the bourgeoisie. It would have been wrapped around the waist several times and could be worn either way around.
58b8041e-0838-56a2-b0b3-2369a498e868.method_for_datation: By its decoration, the length and width of the belt and the flexibility of the fabric.
58b8041e-0838-56a2-b0b3-2369a498e868.method_for_provenance: According to the studies carried out on the subject and the work of historians, brocade workshops were set up in Fez from the Marinid era until the early 20th century.

593969dc-7368-5182-961d-c81a464474fc.name: Bridal headdress (*Kiska*)
593969dc-7368-5182-961d-c81a464474fc.short_description: Hairpins and other articles of adornment worn on the head were inevitable elements of Macedonian women's attire in the 19th century and at the beginning of the 20th century. This distinctive decorative pin – *kiska* – was used for supporting the hat or scarf. This type of jewellery also conveyed a symbolic meaning and served an apotropaic purpose in addition to its decorative function. The pear-shaped ornament was made by application of filigree and granulation techniques. It is adorned with pellets and decorative stones in varied colours. Tiny coins are suspended on chains at the bottom of the ornament.

59e106e1-b0a2-5505-af4e-7abfde04a90a.name: Belt
59e106e1-b0a2-5505-af4e-7abfde04a90a.short_description: Leather belt embellished with silver pieces decorated in niello with patterns and symbols at the end. Two silver rosette buckles at the end form a locking mechanism. This is an object produced by Circassian craftsmen. The immigration of the Circassians to the Ottoman Empire started in the middle of 19th century and continued until 1900. The Circassian communities migrated mostly to the eastern Arab countries, with which they had spiritual and religious links. They brought with them their traditional activities, crafts and decorative patterns. All these elements soon mingled with the local Arab society and became part of the social and economic landscape of the Arab countries.

5d9fc24f-9c51-56b2-a925-33389c038005.name: Paper crown for *Maulid an-Nabi*
5d9fc24f-9c51-56b2-a925-33389c038005.short_description: In Egypt, houses are festively decorated for the Prophet's birthday, the *Maulid an-Nabi*, and the mosques are brightly lit. Jugglers, fire-swallowers and dancing Sufis fill the streets and squares of Cairo. Processions snake through the streets. Children are treated to carousel rides. Merchants appear and sell a variety of figures made out of sugar, wrapped with coloured paper; that are particularly popular with children. Another hit amongst the children is a birthday crown, made out of cardboard, printed tissue paper and wire, on the forehead of which is displayed a paper image, cut out of a newspaper, of an *ʿud* (lute) player, or a famous star from film and television. Gifts given at the festival of *Maulid* are made of ephemeral, perishable materials such as paper. These are small works of art full of poetry and definite meaning. *Ephemera* are intended for shortterm use as they are unsuitable for prolonged use in daily life.

5ea5b8ab-9f07-5718-8f32-a6c53d04b318.name: Tunic.
5ea5b8ab-9f07-5718-8f32-a6c53d04b318.description:
This tunic is dyed black. It has a rounded collar and half-length sleeves. The garment opens at the back and can only be donned by first putting the hand into the sleeves. It was probably made for a child and is similar in design to contemporary Coptic clothing. The embroidery occurs where the sleeves join the body and is different on each side.  
The right-hand band has a red background on which yellow lines form geometric shapes. These are interspersed with medallion shapes containing stylised vegetable, floral and animal motifs, some could be hares.  
In the left-hand band the colours are more varied and the motifs are animal; mainly hares and dogs in blue, green and black. The background is yellow. The two bands are framed with pious inscriptions in angular *kufic* lettering embroidered in silk. Although they are damaged and almost illegible, we can read;  
'Lasting blessings \[…\] sovereignty is with God'.
5ea5b8ab-9f07-5718-8f32-a6c53d04b318.short_description: The shape of this linen tunic, dyed black and undoubtedly intended for a child, is reminiscent of Coptic clothes. Each sleeve is decorated around the shoulders slightly differently from the other with plant and floral elements mixed with stylised zoomorphic motifs.
5ea5b8ab-9f07-5718-8f32-a6c53d04b318.dimensions: Length 70 cm, width 50 cm to 70 cm; 120 cm (with sleeves).
5ea5b8ab-9f07-5718-8f32-a6c53d04b318.method_for_datation: Tunics dating from the High Muslim era are rare, and this limits our dating criteria. However, based on the decoration and the type of script, we can date this object fairly accurately from the 3rd–4th / 9th–10th centuries.
5ea5b8ab-9f07-5718-8f32-a6c53d04b318.obtention: This garment was bought from an antique dealership in Cairo in 1958 by H. H. Abdelwahab, former Director of the National Institute of Art and Archaeology. He donated it to the Bardo Museum in 1962.

5f89dbe5-9c2a-5bd5-873c-3b29fca4dd90.name: Coronation mantle
5f89dbe5-9c2a-5bd5-873c-3b29fca4dd90.short_description:
The precious mantle embroidered with gold, pearls and cloisonné-enamelled plaques was part of the set of robes used at the coronations of the kings and emperors of the Holy Roman Empire. The semicircular edge of the mantle is decorated with a gold-embroidered *kufic* inscription. It reveals that the mantle was produced in AH 528/ AD 1133/34 during the reign of the Norman king Roger II of Sicily (AD 1095–1154) in the royal workshops in Palermo where among others Arabic artisans worked.  
Ancient motifs are depicted on the surface of the semicircular mantle: to both sides of a palm-tree (representing the tree of life) a lion triumph over a camel, which has a saddle and bridle and has thus been domesticated.

5f944369-bc84-59f2-a3a6-21c5dda0f6fe.name: Wooden clogs
5f944369-bc84-59f2-a3a6-21c5dda0f6fe.short_description: Wooden clogs such as these have a long history in the Middle East, emerging before the Middle Ages and remaining popular for centuries to come. They were made of a variety of woods, including walnut, apricot, willow, poplar, or beech. The wood was cut into wedge shapes then moulded around the foot of the wearer. Excess wood was then shaved off, the heel attached, and the wood painted and polished. Leather girdles in a variety of colours were fixed to the heel with special nails and the wood would often be decorated with mosaics of bone or seashells organised in geometric or floral patterns. Clogs were designed to be comfortable and resistant to water, and thus were usually worn at home, particularly by women. These shoes have a higher heel than usual and would be worn by brides so that they would appear taller than the other girls in the *hammam* (Turkish baths).

6358ef7b-3436-5d35-ad94-2c51478ff9e5.name: Womanʼs jacket
6358ef7b-3436-5d35-ad94-2c51478ff9e5.short_description:
After 1873, Iranian women of the upper classes wore a short skirt imitating the French *tutu* worn by ballet dancers. Called *shalitah*, this little skirt was combined with a small jacket, kept above the waist so as not to spoil the puffy effect of the *shalitah*, with long sleeves worn over a thin shirt.  
  
As was customary at the time, the outer fabric is a Persian *qalamkar*, a printed fabric that is intricately handmade, whist in contrast, cheap European printed cotton fabrics was used, as was convention, for the lining. However, the two fabrics were not combined at random, and it is clear from the intriguing contrast that much attention was given to the choice of these two patterns. The ogival lattice structure that dominates the Persian print enjoyed a long tradition in Ottoman, Indian and Persian textile design and was even known in the West.  
  
This jacket was acquired by the Swiss merchant Emil Alpiger in Iran between 1870 and 1896. Alpiger was then director of the Manchester-based trading company Ziegler & Co. which owned a carpet factory in Sultanabad.

65b12078-9fc9-543e-94fd-9274d0e1813b.name: Cloak belonging to Sheikh Muhammad al-Khalili.
65b12078-9fc9-543e-94fd-9274d0e1813b.description:
A cloak ('*Aba'a*) or outer garment composed of small pieces (approximately 3 cm x 3 cm) sewn together. The pieces consist of woven silk and cotton stitched together with woollen thread. The background, in the form of polygons, is made up from interchanging colours that include yellow, red, green and black. The polygons are arranged within rectangles tightly woven in an elongated form, which would have made the wearer (Sheikh Muhammad al-Khalili) seem taller in stature than he was in reality. The woven section at the back of the garment between the shoulders is square, containing a circle of polygons arranged in circles, which become smaller by degrees as they move towards the centre of the circle. This gives the back of the cloak great depth and splendour. Two facing triangular sections in the corners of the square are red, while the two other corners are black. The garment has half sleeves finished with a band of green silk. This mode of outer garment was inspired by the asceticism and the piety of its wearer. It is made from very small pieces of cloth to make it appear as if it was woven from pieces of fabric. The Sheikh's cloak is considered a rarity, having survived in a complete state and in such beautiful condition.  
Sheikh Muhammad al-Khalili was among the scholars of *fiqh* (Islamic Jurisprudence) in Jerusalem and one of the most important personalities of Palestine at the time. In view of his distinctive position he was buried in the Madrasa al-Ashrafiyya located at the western wall of the Haram al-Sharif. This honour was bestowed on a select group which did not exceed 10 Islamic personalities over the course of history. Sheikh al-Khalili was renowned for wearing this cloak which was preserved for more than two centuries in his burial chamber until it was transferred to the Islamic Museum.

It covered his tomb. It is woven from small polygonal pieces in cotton and silk. The coat has half sleeves. This garment is a rare example to have survived almost completely intact.

69944391-4804-5b5b-96e7-56b15185e288.name: Kaftan fragment.
69944391-4804-5b5b-96e7-56b15185e288.description:
A silk brocade (*kemha*) fragment that originally formed the front of a child's collarless, short-sleeved kaftan, cut with a straight waist and bell-shaped skirt. The textile is woven with a dense, overall design of undulating vines and floral detail in subtle gold and greenish-brown hues, set against a cream-coloured background.  
The original museum record states that this piece represents a portion of a child's robe-of-honour from Constantinople or Bursa. Possibly arriving in Turkey via Syria, the complex weaving technique adopted on this textile, known as lampas weave, was used by Ottoman weavers in the late AH 9th–early 10th /AD late 15th–early 16th century. The most important Ottoman silk manufactory was at Bursa but in the AH 10th / AD 16th century, court workshops were also set up in Istanbul, the Ottoman capital. *Kemha* garments were designed to emphasise the imperial status of the sultan and his family even in death, when such garments were often draped over imperial cenotaphs or *sanduka*s.  
This fragment is part of a group of garments that was brought to Europe by an art dealer and cut up with some of the resulting front and back sections subsequently divided between the V&A in London and the Royal Museum in Edinburgh.

6b03ecfa-3333-5fb8-b1a6-fd52388b653a.name: Textile fragment.
6b03ecfa-3333-5fb8-b1a6-fd52388b653a.description:
This is a fragment from a shawl or turban made from fine linen and decorated with a wide band of delicately woven vegetal decoration in green, blue and yellow silk. In the lower portion of this band, is a line of inscription in *kufic* script woven in brown silk that reads: 'In the name of God, the Blessings of God on Abd Allah al-Amin Muhammad, Commander of the Faithful, may God grant him a long life, who has commissioned the production of this in the *tiraz al-'amma* \[…\] Egypt at the hands of al-Fadl bin al-Rabi', a supporter of the Commander of the Faithful'.This is considered to be the oldest woven silk inscription on linen. In the Islamic-period a shawl or turban, such as the one from which this fragment comes, was usually decorated at both ends by a decorative band next to which was a band of inscription, and then a thin strip; the shawl or turban would have been finished with a fringe.  
This piece was made in *tiraz al-'amma* (the public workshop). Beside the public *tiraz*, there were textile establishments which were set up by the caliphs to produce garments and textiles for the caliph and his entourage; these were called *tiraz al-khasa* (exclusive workshops). Some of the fine *tiraz al-'amma* textiles, indicate that these were commissioned when needed by the caliphs alongside *tiraz al-khasa*. The storehouses of the Abbasid Caliph, Muhammad al-Amin (r. AH 193–8 / AD 809–13) were filled with clothes, hangings and carpets, to the point where it took al-Fadl ibn Rabi' four months to complete the inventory of the contents of these treasuries, demonstrating the great interest that this caliph took in a variety of apparel, turbans and coverings.
6b03ecfa-3333-5fb8-b1a6-fd52388b653a.short_description: This fragment bears the name of the Abbasid Caliph al-Amin Muhammad and is considered to be the oldest woven silk inscription on linen. The Fatimids established many government textile factories called *Tiraz*. Some specialised in making textiles for the caliph and his court; others were allocated for the general public.
6b03ecfa-3333-5fb8-b1a6-fd52388b653a.method_for_datation: The textile is dated based on the mention of the Abbasid caliph, Muhammad al-Amin and his follower al-Fadl ibn al-Rabi' in the inscription band which embellishes this textile fragment.
6b03ecfa-3333-5fb8-b1a6-fd52388b653a.method_for_provenance: It is thought that Fustat is the most likely place of production in view of the fact that Egypt is mentioned as the place of manufacture in the inscription band.
6b03ecfa-3333-5fb8-b1a6-fd52388b653a.obtention: This piece was bought in 1903, from an antiquities dealer, Paul Philip.

6b90a9c0-f193-55c4-9a03-d29b7b481484.name: *Kiswah* Belt
6b90a9c0-f193-55c4-9a03-d29b7b481484.short_description:
Religious leaders in the Muslim world would commission the crafting of the *Kiswah* - the cover of the Kaaba - including key components such this belt embellished in gold and silver thread. Craftsmen embroider Qur’anic verses and words of protective value to provide a generous offering to the house of God. This belt was manufactured in Egypt.  
  
Once a new veil is bestowed upon the cubic building, the previous cover is broken up beneath the new *Kiswah* and donated to individuals and institutions such as museums to honor the yearly tradition.

703b6c7e-f4d6-51d7-9caa-1fade8284326.name: Bejewelled ivory belts.
703b6c7e-f4d6-51d7-9caa-1fade8284326.description:
Two ivory belts, one comprising five large plaques with oval medallions, and the other four large plaques with round medallions, attached to each other with groups of small conjoined rectangular pieces. All are decorated in multiple layers. The surfaces are decorated with finely engraved spiralling tendrils and flower motifs, their lines filled with black mastic. The second layer of decoration includes gold flowers with rubies and turquoises at their centres, connected to tendrils with golden leaves. The background is concealed under the all-pervasive decoration, and the base materials are outshone by the ostentatiously encrusted stones. The deeply inlaid flowers in gilded settings, and the technique of decoration in multiple layers, reflect the courtly art of jewellery during the reign of Süleyman the Magnificent (r. AH 926–74 / AD 1520–66).  
  
The organisations of court artists and artisans (called the Ehl-i Hiref) were founded in the reign of Bayezid II (r. AH 886–918 / AD 1481–1512) and these organisations served as a school for all fields of Ottoman art. The number of artists at work in the palace can be followed from the books of salaries, which were kept regularly beginning in the reign of Süleyman the Magnificent.  
  
A popular accessory for both men and women, belts were used to enrich and decorate a costume, secured around the waist. They bore a ritual meaning as well. Promotion to a certain rank was completed with the ceremony of girding on a belt. This custom, known from professional guilds was important for the sultans as well, and it was emphasised by placing a belt on the cenotaphs of deceased sultans and courtiers. In the Ottoman period, belts were produced from precious textiles and embroidered with silver and gold threads. Carved and ornamented belts made from metal plaques fitted side by side exhibit high standards of craftsmanship. While women's belts were elaborately decorated, those worn by men were fairly plain.
703b6c7e-f4d6-51d7-9caa-1fade8284326.short_description: In the Ottoman period, belts were used not only as accessories for women's and men's costumes, but were also palatial awards given for promotion to a higher rank or for remarkable professional accomplishments in a 'belt girding' ceremony.

77e732d5-caee-5472-847f-63e657f1353d.name: Kaftan fragment.
77e732d5-caee-5472-847f-63e657f1353d.description:
A silk brocade (*kemha*) fragment that originally formed the back of a child's collarless, short-sleeved kaftan, cut with a straight waist and bell-shaped skirt. The textile is woven with a dense overall design of eight-pointed stars in staggered rows. Each star contains a central motif, consisting of eight tulip heads issuing from a central rosette. Tri-lobed arabesque extensions enhance the stars at the top and bottom. This type of pattern is also found in Ottoman velvets.  
The original museum record states that this piece represents a portion of a child's robe-of-honour from Constantinople or Bursa. Possibly arriving in Turkey via Syria, the complex weaving technique adopted on this textile, known as lampas weave, was used by Ottoman weavers in the late AH 9th–early 10th /AD late 15th–early 16th century. The most important Ottoman silk manufactory was at Bursa but in the AH 10th / AD 16th century, court workshops were also set up in Istanbul, the Ottoman capital. *Kemha* garments were designed to emphasise the imperial status of the sultan and his family even in death, when such garments were often draped over imperial cenotaphs or *sanduka*s.  
This fragment is part of a group of garments that was brought to Europe by an art dealer and cut up with some of the resulting front and back sections subsequently divided between the V&A in London and the Royal Museum in Edinburgh.
77e732d5-caee-5472-847f-63e657f1353d.short_description: Royal child kaftans were among the products made in the Imperial Ottoman silk weaving centres at Bursa and Istanbul. The silk brocadecostumes were designed to emphasise the imperial status of the sultan and his family, even in death when such garments were often draped over imperial cenotaphs or *sandukas*.
77e732d5-caee-5472-847f-63e657f1353d.dates: Hegira, late 10th–early 11th century / AD late 16th– early 17th century.
77e732d5-caee-5472-847f-63e657f1353d.method_for_datation: *Kemha* textiles were popular in the Ottoman Empire between the late 10th–early 11th / late 16th–early 17th centuries.

79528dd8-b305-5d0a-99c2-94a3c8d75553.name: Clogs
79528dd8-b305-5d0a-99c2-94a3c8d75553.description: *Nanule* (Tr. *nalın*) – clogs from the Museum of Applied Art in Belgrade (a.n. TC-283 (1942)), are made of wood. They have a slightly flared front wedge and a concave back wedge. The toe of the sole is square, and the heel is round. The sole is decorated with intarsia of leaf-shaped medallions with carved vegetal motifs, while along the edges runs a frame of inlaid mother-of-pearl rhombi. The wedges are adorned with carved geometrical motifs. The leather straps that hold the clog on the foot are plain. The clogs were used in the hamam, and belong to the shared dress and living culture of the urban population in the Ottoman Balkans, which had diverse confessional and ethnic backgrounds.

79fded3c-fc12-5fa3-bff4-6820a231b3e4.name: Marriage shawl
79fded3c-fc12-5fa3-bff4-6820a231b3e4.short_description: This loose marriage shawl is decorated with various symbols of fertility. Two large rectangles of red wool are sewn together, and their joining seam is ornately decorated with gold embroidery. The decorations are spread out across the whole cloth, forming a strip of finely woven motifs in the centre, which is surrounded by various traditional figures and patterns. The human figures are characteristic of the (often enigmatic) decorative arts of the towns of El Jem and Ouerdanine, and feature here in addition to the more common motifs such as the fish, the hand, disks, circles, diamonds, crescents, the dove and the camel.

7c5b0aa9-383a-5b52-bc5a-91c986d3c9eb.name: Toiletries
7c5b0aa9-383a-5b52-bc5a-91c986d3c9eb.short_description: In the 19th century the wealthy families of Tunis invented the notion of the knastrou l'aroussa (marriage basket) as a mark of their wealth. Made of engraved or watermarked silver, this basket would contain various toiletries for the bride: a perfume sprinkler (mrach), a khol phial with applicator for the eyes (mokhala), a round or rectangular-framed mirror with engraved floral motifs, and a knife and plate for henna. A pair of clogs (qobqabs) made of wood and covered in silver worn by the bride. As a traditional bath (hammam) was the bride's first event on her wedding day, all her toiletries were set out ready for her, with a series of tools for exfoliation, depilation, application of a clay face mask, and more.

80deca91-898b-5c5f-bbd8-e342f80ead7f.name: Burqa - Face Cover
80deca91-898b-5c5f-bbd8-e342f80ead7f.short_description:
A rare example of a traditional accessory that adorns nomadic women during special occasions such as weddings, the decorated veil remains a source of honour and identity for Bedouins. It is found across the Middle East, especially in Egypt’s Sinai region, southern Palestine, and the Tabuk region of north-western Saudi Arabia. The veil reflects the shared material culture and long-standing historical interactions across Sinai, the southern Levant, and north-western Arabia.  
  
Shells, colourful beads and over 350 gold and silver coins adorn this burgundy veil, revealing only the eyes while the burgundy fabric masks the nose, mouth and neck. In a shiny coat of feathers, the coins aim to reflect ill intent, with the Maria Theresa thaler as a central display of wealth and status. Triangle and diamond shapes embody amulet-like powers in thoughtful cross-stitching and beadwork. As a final touch, cowrie shells defend against the evil eye and enhance fertility through their suggestive resemblance.

84d4fca3-e4d2-596e-bea2-0a5eda7a5ccf.name: Traditional dress for a *shaykh* or *shaykha*
84d4fca3-e4d2-596e-bea2-0a5eda7a5ccf.short_description: Featured here is the traditional dress for the *shaykh* and *shaykha* of the Keserwan district. The *kubran* is an embroidered jacket (with or without sleeves) made of silk or velvet. The *gumbaz* is a long dress or coat embroidered with gold or silver and sometimes adorned with semi-precious jewels. It consisted of three panels and was split on either side of the body, beginning from the hip area. Other components of this traditional attire were a *mentiene* (blouse), the *shirwal* baggy trousers, a velvet or satin cape with gold or silver embroidery, and a long belt called a *shamle* or *zunnar* made of silk or cashmere depending on the season, and which was wrapped around the waist or hips.

8965ef4e-0491-5348-8ff0-02681f79580f.name: Woman’s court robe (*conteş*)
8965ef4e-0491-5348-8ff0-02681f79580f.short_description: This *seraser* silk was discovered in the latter half of the nineteenth century in a monastery located in the historical region of Oltenia (southwestern Romania), probably at Bistriţa, where it was preserved as an ecclesiastical cope. A hundred years later, following ample restoration undertaken at the Museum, it regained its original form, namely that of a woman’s court robe. It can be assumed that the robe had been donated to the monastery by a boyar’s family, which testifies to the wealth and refinement of the Romanian aristocracy in the sixteenth century, given the fact that *seraser* silk was by far the most precious Ottoman textile, covered ‘from end to end’ with silver and silver-gilt thread. The robe features a design of large palmette garlands, outlined with green silk, each of which encloses a circular motif and a crescent. Between the garlands, circular motifs surrounding a star.

The artist’s palette of brilliant color, graphic design, and combination of textures resulted in costumes markedly different from the originals. Cleopatra’s luminous dress, reflecting the abstract forms in Sonia Delaunay’s paintings, as well as aspects of fashionable dress of the period, remains one of her most significant creations for the theatre.

The fineness of workmanship indicates a production in the context of the Court. The sleeves are overlong, slit below and lined with embroidered top fabric. The dress is fastened in the middle more or less to the waist with twelve ornamentally trimmed buttons. The tambour embroidery includes floral scrolls and bunches of flowers as well as miniature architectural motifs and birds.

8c4076d1-62c9-5729-a3d5-d8c91345437b.name: Bridal headdress
8c4076d1-62c9-5729-a3d5-d8c91345437b.description: An example of coin-adorned accessories from Palestine dating to the early twentieth century, this bridal headdress originates from the villages of the Jaffa area. The coins incorporated into bridal ornaments symbolised part of the bride’s dowry, traditionally gifted by the groom’s family and considered her personal property, which she could keep and use according to her wishes. The embroidered motifs and techniques featured on the headdress are characteristic of the Jaffa region’s village dress traditions and are also found on women’s garments from the area.

8d188108-655f-550e-b130-a0eb24f32b9c.name: Headdress
8d188108-655f-550e-b130-a0eb24f32b9c.short_description: Three bands of silver (800) chain fitted around the sides and over the crown of the head; 1/4 Ottoman coins (*barah*s) are fixed in the inner section of the band. This kind of jewellery was part of the dowry the groom gave to the bride. Dowries consisted mostly of silver jewellery because only the rich could afford gold jewellery. Thus, the financial status of the groom was highlighted by the jewellery he could give as a dowry and by the use of coins as pieces of jewellery for his wife.

901912af-e2dd-5692-a2e7-be09e9e75334.name: 'Abaya-style dress
901912af-e2dd-5692-a2e7-be09e9e75334.description: This ‘abaya style dress incorporates a variety of fabrics sourced from all over the world brought together into a vibrant yet harmonious piece.   Colourful Indian and Southeast Asian textiles in the form of silk ikats and brocaded sari borders sit alongside embroidered suzani panels from Central Asia and plain coloured textiles sourced in the United Kingdom or the Middle East.  Designed by Thea Porter for Thea Porter Couture, this garment harked exoticism.  In line with fashion trends of the 1970s, designers such as Porter looked to Middle Eastern, South Asian and Central Asian textiles for inspiration, incorporating them into their designs. Such bright textiles with their vibrant colour combinations, textures, and bold patterns spoke to notions of travel to exotic destination, highlighted exposure to different cultures, and in an era of synthetic fibres, placed emphasis on natural materials and the handmade.  Born in Jerusalem but having lived in Damascus and Beirut, Porter introduced her Western clientèle to voluminous Arab-style over-garments such as ‘abayas and thawbs.    Her loose shapes and her innate understanding and choice of fabrics appealed to many with Porter being credited with bringing the bohemian look to London catwalks.
