922e411d-1b69-5d14-ac14-e76be57376fa.name: Kaftan.
922e411d-1b69-5d14-ac14-e76be57376fa.description:
A woman's garment, rectangular in shape, widening slightly towards the top and open at the front with long, wide sleeves. Braided conical buttons fasten the garment at the top.  
The word 'kaftan' was originally Persian and was adopted by the Ottomans to describe their emperor's dress. It would have been introduced in Morocco by the Sa'did king 'Abd al-Malik (r. AH 984–6 / AD 1576–8), who had lived in Algiers and Istanbul and would have borrowed the word from the Turks. Adopted firstly by the dignitaries and women of the palace, kaftans became fashionable among the middle classes from the late AH 10th / AD 17th century, if the accounts of European travellers are to be believed. Each of the large towns had a particular variation of this type of costume, which would have been covered with a light tunic. Its shape and decoration tell us that this kaftan is from Tetouan. It would not have been hidden under a tunic and would have been worn above a bolero made in the same way and in the same material. Embroidered with gold thread, gold braids and frogging, its arborescent decoration is reminiscent of the designs on the dresses and boleros of Ottoman women in Algeria.
922e411d-1b69-5d14-ac14-e76be57376fa.short_description: This woman's garment is rectangular and slightly opened at the front. It would have been worn above a bolero, and the braided buttons fastened the top of the garment. Its gold thread and gold braiding decoration would have been inspired by the clothes worn by Ottoman women in Algiers.

922e411d-1b69-5d14-ac14-e76be57376fa.method_for_datation: This type of kaftan was produced only in Tetouan and was worn only by middle-class women in the north of Morocco.
922e411d-1b69-5d14-ac14-e76be57376fa.method_for_provenance: This type of kaftan was no longer worn at the beginning of the 20th century.

92dacff0-b9ed-51f4-8929-313eefaa5ba9.short_description: This Bedouin shirt from Palmyra, Syria was collected by an Austrian officer named Karl Alexander Anselm Freiherr von Hügel. He left the army in 1824 and organized a long voyage, which took him from France to the Near East. He first visited Syria and Palestine, then reached Mumbai, India in 1832. 94c59dc9-5032-599d-bcf3-18eec377e4fa.name: Velvet embroidered kaftan
94c59dc9-5032-599d-bcf3-18eec377e4fa.short_description: This purple velvet kaftan is decorated with gold and silver braided trimmings and embroidered with silver and golden metal thread. It is fitted with mid-length sleeves embellished with a large "lyonnais" ribbon. The chest is covered by a large breastplate, split into two symmetrical halves, and adorned with large buttons of gold lace. The embroidery on the breastplate features two peacocks facing, on each side, a bowl with floral motifs. The kaftan is lined with a pale blue satinette on the outer rims with a pattern of swallows' wings sewn on. The kaftan, a particularly lavish item in the 19th century, was typically worn for marriage ceremonies, usually with calf-length trousers.

9729e384-0aab-59c6-bb73-2a5621d81218.name: Bridal headdress (*Tepelak* – tas)
9729e384-0aab-59c6-bb73-2a5621d81218.short_description: Jewellery worn on the head included diverse types of metal articles which served to support the hat or scarf and also had an apotropaic function in addition to their decorative one. Especially noteworthy head-pieces were *tepelaks*. These are headdresses of round form, sometimes slightly concave, abundantly adorned with chains, smaller or larger silver coins and with *trepkas* (tiny ornaments in diverse forms – round, leaf-shaped, rectangular, heart-shaped, etc.). *Tepelaks* used to be worn everywhere in Macedonia, particularly in the Kumanovo, Skopje, Gostivar and Gevgelija regions, as well as within Vlachs. This piece of bridal *tepelak-tas* was made by application of filigree technique. It is abundantly decorated with coins suspended on tiny chains.

97603dc7-78b0-567d-995d-706683438f46.name: Wedding dress
97603dc7-78b0-567d-995d-706683438f46.short_description: The main fabric of this wedding dress is linen with silk selvedge stripes, with red and yellow taffeta inserts in the sleeves and skirt; the chest panel is couched with gilt cord and yellow, green and purple silk cord, and filled with multi-coloured stain and herringbone stitches. Palestinian weavers used manual spindles to prepare the cotton and linen threads imported from Egypt. Ashkelon weavers used light vertical hand looms (*Majdalawi* looms) to produce linen fabrics, while silk fabrics were spindled, died and woven in Syria. The Jordanian economy in the late 19th and early 20th centuries relied on trade and crafts; new waves of people started to come to Jordan to participate in those industries. This object shows the diverse population composition of Jordan at that time, through personal attire, fashion, local costumes and rites.

9a135c4c-830c-5fdd-a5e6-61129754ecfd.name: Bridal breast jewellery (*Chaprag*)
9a135c4c-830c-5fdd-a5e6-61129754ecfd.short_description: This exquisite article called a *chaprag* shows the exceptional skill and inventiveness of the unknown goldsmith, who makes each piece of jewellery a virtual work of art in itself. The *chaprag* is a breast ornament consisting of a round plate and tiny chains. It is executed in filigree technique and adorned with decorative stones. Besides its decorative function, it was applied for the purpose of fastening the cleavage of the tunic. It was characteristic of the Ohrid-Prespa region, that is, the areas of Ohridsko Pole, Strushko Pole and Debarski Drimkol.

9aa9bf06-9414-5502-8c25-a49ce6269462.name: Belt
9aa9bf06-9414-5502-8c25-a49ce6269462.short_description: A Circassian belt with 15 silver and niello-decorated buckles connected together to form the belt; there is a rosette shape at the end with locking mechanism and three dangling silver tassels. This belt, together with the dagger, was an accessory forming the traditional male Circassian dress. The Circassians used to carry daggers which were an essential part of the national dress. The immigration of the Circassians to the Ottoman Empire started in the middle of 19th century and continued until 1900. The Circassian communities migrated mostly to the eastern Arab countries with which they had spiritual and religious links.

9d7d8f95-c69d-5158-8fc8-44463428b5eb.description: From the 1970s to the 1990s, important figures in fashion like Ursula Rodel, Ruth Grüninger, Hannes Bühler, Ida Gut, and Dorothee Vogel influenced the Swiss designer Christa de Carouge whose work represented a new departure for Swiss fashion. 9e27b5b2-30a6-5252-a26a-4aac66765be3.name: Silk coat
9e27b5b2-30a6-5252-a26a-4aac66765be3.short_description:
The coat is made of two patterned textiles. The first, a fine late-Sasanian samite with a design of roundels enclosing a peacock in profile, is used mainly around the edges (textile A). The second, a samite of medium quality with a design of roundels enclosing a peacock presented frontally, forms the principal parts of the coat and was most probably made by Iranian weavers working in China (textile B). The lining, which survives mostly in the sleeves, is a purplish-brown self-patterned tabby silk of Chinese origin, (textile C). Its design is based on overlapping ovals enclosing a seated ruler, paired animals or birds and a fantastic animal, perhaps a dragon. In addition, two plain tabby fabrics are used as a facing inside the extremities of the coat and an interlining for the collar. Alterations to the coat appear to have involved adding the second samite, textile B, so that it became the its principal textile.  
Although these precious samites have been cut up into much smaller pieces than should have been necessary, this kind of garment construction is evidently a common feature among finds from Dulan, the site from which the coat almost certainly comes.  
**Additions to dating**  
Textile A  
C-14 dating: AD 533–615 (87.4% probability). Because of its evolved design, the actual date must be closer to the end of this range.  
Textile B  
C-14 dating: two date ranges, AD 430–93 and AD 530–96 (95.4% probability). The actual date is more likely to be at the upper end of the second range, close to 600 AD.  
Textile C  
The approximate date of this lining silk can be estimated as c. 600 AD, because a yellow fragment with the same weave and design was found in a tomb at Astana, near Turfan, with documents dating between AD 541–622.

9f475267-426c-5190-b0b3-f114b5dfce94.name: Embroidered Safavid coat
9f475267-426c-5190-b0b3-f114b5dfce94.short_description: The voluminous men’s coat reaching half way down the thighs is embroidered with a pattern of figures, cypresses, blossoming trees and small ponds. Enthroned men under baldachins are each flanked by a guard with bow and arrow and a woman carrying a peacock. Comparable motifs on textiles and in sixteenth-century miniatures show that the elaborately designed type of garment was widespread. Similar exquisite articles of clothing served as gifts of the rulers to their retinue and were usually not intended for daily use.

9ff5077e-cf93-5273-8105-87762d317700.name: *Ihram* belt
9ff5077e-cf93-5273-8105-87762d317700.short_description:
This *ihram* belt would have been worn by a male pilgrim, and used for carrying valuables while performing the Hajj rites. The *ihram* garment for men consists of two pieces of unstitched white cloth. One cloth (the *rida’*) is worn around the upper body while the other (the *izar*) would be worn wrapped around the lower body. This belt would have been worn around the waist on top of the *izar*. The inscription upon the belt wishes the wearer good health.  
As well as referring to ritual clothing, *ihram* also donates a state of mind in which a Muslim must enter in order to embark on Hajj. During this period, pilgrims must adhere to certain rules, for instance men and women are both forbidden from killing animals, uprooting trees, or cutting their nails or hair.

a21ee902-973e-5d31-8729-1620d2b89aae.name: Kaftan.
a21ee902-973e-5d31-8729-1620d2b89aae.description:
The red caftan with its wide sleeves is part of the costume of an Algerian woman. The fine, shiny silk shows a floral pattern of large blossoms and leaves. The gold-thread embroidery of the neckline and on both sides of the buttons is the only additional ornamentation. The sparing but effective use of the gold thread and the contrast of the colours emphasise the precious character of this garment.  
Together with headdress and shoes, this kaftan was part of a large gift presented by Ali Pasha of Algiers to the Swedish king in AH 1144 / AD 1731 in connection with the peace treaty between Sweden and Algeria.

a2ba32a3-7747-5b54-b011-e71d3a84e08c.description: Pink silk twill dress lined with cotton, long-sleeved and high-waisted. The neckline is round in the front and triangle-shaped in the back. The upper bodice area is boned. Both breasts are marked with a U-shaped pleating. The skirt is soberly straight in front but it gains volume towards the back, ending in a short trail. The dress is fastened with invisible hooks at the back and adorned with buttons covered in the same silk fabric. The lower end presents a wide multi-coloured paisley frieze; each drop is composed of minute woven flowers. This elegant dress is a late variation of Empire dresses; the slender high-waisted silhouette is the same, but the fabric is thicker, the neckline has turned more modest and the long sleeves go down to cover part of the hands.

a2f41b51-30af-503a-a290-05cb553751f2.name: Part of a veil
a2f41b51-30af-503a-a290-05cb553751f2.short_description: Five lines of gold ¼ Ottoman lira and other type of coins sewn together on a piece of cloth; such pieces were usually affixed above the nose on the veils, *burqu'*, of women of Beer Sheba. Fashion, local costumes and rites in the territories of Jordan and Palestine show identical elements, as this veil illustrates. It is one of the many examples of jewellery made with Ottoman coins to decorate veils and dresses. Jewellery was an important accessory for married women because pieces of jewellery constituted part of the dowry their husbands gave them for marriage. Jewellery was also a symbol of financial prestige: the more precious it was, the richer the husband’s family. Silver jewellery was the most common because only rich people could afford gold jewellery.

a399cdfb-dda0-5b17-89ab-56d6fc1c5bcb.name: A *chādri* grill
a399cdfb-dda0-5b17-89ab-56d6fc1c5bcb.short_description:
This grill dates from the early 20th century. It is embroidered with flowers, with the names of Allah, Muhammad, Fatima, Hasan and Husayn, and with the Muslim declaration of belief.  
In 1997, the religious police decreed all women in Afghanistan must wear the *chādri* in public. This brought about a significant change for women. Women who were improperly covered outside their home were punished severely, along with their family elders, or risked being beaten in public by Taliban militiamen. In present-day Europe, migrant communities’ legitimate demands for equal representation of their religious values and symbols has aroused a counter-discourse, mainly led by populist politicians, against the cultural and religious demands of pluralism. Due to the increasing presence of Islam in the public sphere the *chādri* and other items of Islamic/Islamist women’s clothing are no longer seen as a mere signs of subservience but have shifted to become symbols of terrorism.

a46e6bab-37d1-5f3c-a753-4f870c27eaf0.name: Babouches [slippers] given to the King of Italy by an Ambassador from Morocco visiting Italy in 1890
a46e6bab-37d1-5f3c-a753-4f870c27eaf0.short_description:
In 1890, the Sultan of Morocco sent Hagi El Maati el Mazamizi as an ambassador to Italy. The Ambassador landed in Naples on June 7th and arrived by train in Rome on June 13th. At the railway station he was received by the Mayor or Rome, the Prefect, and other authorities. A military band was playing and military men in high uniform were paraded in the station to greet the Ambassador.  
Outside the station, three of the King’s gala carriages were waiting for the Ambassador and a military unit was paraded in his honour. Some carabinieri in high uniform escorted the Ambassador to the hotel.  
Hagi El Maati el Mazamizi presented the King with gifts, including some superb horses that the King immensely appreciated. The King presented the Ambassador with a magnificent small gold and diamond box and a hunting rifle and gave gold watches to the members of his escort.

It carries extensive embroidery executed in gold-coloured metal thread, highlighting in particular the collar, the edges of the garment and the side pockets. Further ornamentation enhances the back. In the context of rising nationalisms, traditional costume played an important role, both in Europe and – to a lesser extent – in the Middle East. This waist coat may originally have been made in one of the European provinces of the Ottoman Empire, as it shows certain similarities with costume from the Balkans.

ae76a20b-77b1-575a-ab1c-36776cb0c633.name: Fragment of a robe.
ae76a20b-77b1-575a-ab1c-36776cb0c633.description:
This fragment shows two dark blue friezes facing each other, each featuring white *kufic* inscriptions surrounded by pink tendrils with white blossoms. A third frieze, composed of red rosettes with white four-petalled flowers, and framed on either side with waves of brown tendrils on a green background, sits between the two inscription friezes.  
This small fragment, which originally formed part of a much larger *tiraz* band, was identified as having been commissioned for the Fatimid ruler Al-Mustansir billah by comparing it with a similar inscription on a nearly identical piece in the Victoria and Albert Museum, London. The *kufic* text in the upper frieze on the Berlin fragment reads ‘In the name of God the merciful and good. There is no God other than God. M(ohammed is the envoy of God)’. This represents, therefore, the message of Islam. The text in the lower frieze reads ‘…this was commissioned by the vizier, the great…’. The term *tiraz* was derived from the name of the workshops where the cloths with the inscriptions, the *tiraz*, were woven. These robes of honour were manufactured for caliphs and high-ranking nobles in the workshops of the royal court. The *tiraz* were given to local or foreign high-ranking persons as a reward for their services. Medieval sources referred to them as valuable objects. The majority of *tiraz* bands come from Egypt, as these fabrics were preserved very well in the very dry climate and, if buried, the extremely dry earth.
ae76a20b-77b1-575a-ab1c-36776cb0c633.short_description: Cotton textiles with silk embroidery were produced in court workshops in Fatimid Egypt and were called *tiraz* because of the inscriptions which often gave the name of the workshop and the ruler. On special occasions they were presented to people who had rendered services to the state.
ae76a20b-77b1-575a-ab1c-36776cb0c633.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
ae76a20b-77b1-575a-ab1c-36776cb0c633.method_for_datation: An inscription on a similar piece of fabric in the Victoria and Albert Museum, London, into which the name of the Fatimid Caliph Al-Mustansir billah (r. 427–487 / 1036–94) is woven, places this object within the same reign.
ae76a20b-77b1-575a-ab1c-36776cb0c633.method_for_provenance: Comparisons with other fabrics have proved that the two nearly identical fragments – the London one inscribed with the name of the Caliph al-Mustansir billah and the Berlin one – have been produced in a royal workshop in Egypt from which caliphs commissioned the creation of their cloths.

ae7c39ba-6ec7-52c7-ab26-aa458671c2ad.short_description: Bursa was an important hub of trade for Iranian silk and developed into a leading centre for the production of silk fabrics. As such, it did not only purvey to the Ottoman Court; silks from Bursa were coveted export goods for Europe, as is shown by this chasuble. At the same time, Italian silks were very much in demand in the Ottoman Empire. One consequence of this intensive exchange is seen in a reciprocal influencing of motifs, so that frequently technical details are the only characteristics that tell us where the silk fabric was woven, in Italy or in the Ottoman Empire.

b5c0d18b-e693-55ac-b0f0-5d2195dc1c3e.description: Child's kaftan with *agremán* (tape of braids used as adornment), done in fabric brocade of mauve colour. The brocade is decorated with flower medallions with centres of golden thread. The sleeves are short and straight. The edge of the sleeves and of the whole jacket is edged with dark blue silk tape. The front, sides and shoulders are edged in a golden *agremán*, which ends in a circle. The jacket is lined with white cotton fabric and edged by a red tape. This garment was probably worn by children in the circumcision ceremony ritual. The practice of circumcision in the Islamic world involved a ritual in which the children involved in the ceremony were richly dressed.

b6582e55-7f8a-5fe9-9368-5ce8c476126c.name: Dress.
b6582e55-7f8a-5fe9-9368-5ce8c476126c.description:
A modern Palestinian dress cut and embroidered in the traditional way, using imported machine-woven fabric and threads. The embroidery motifs are copied from European pattern books. The simple cross-stitch is implemented with multi-shade coloured cotton threads, giving the motifs a multicoloured and shaded rendering.  
  
The earliest examples of Palestinian needlework to survive were made early in the AH 13th / AD 19th century. These examples are broadly divided into two main regional styles: Galilee and southern Palestine. Arab village women were taught by their mothers to embroider their own garments, and began to learn the craft from the age of six years. A woman's first complete set of costumes would have been her wedding trousseau. The fabrics were either plain cotton or linen, woven locally by male weavers, or imported from Egypt and Greece. The embroidery was mainly used as decoration for dresses, caps and headscarves, with designs made up of combinations of geometrical and floral motifs. These designs and patterns were influenced by similar examples in Syria and Turkey, and in Cyprus and Greece, indicating an active cultural exchange between all sides. Palestinian women were always borrowing and adapting designs from all around them, constantly expanding their repertoire of motifs, and integrating new ones into their traditional schemes.  
  
Although there have been many attempts at attributing symbolic significance to the many motifs used, in general, these patterns did not have such special meanings. However, the embroiderers did give their patterns names to distinguish them, some of which matched the shapes of the patterns, but many others did not.

ba3d1a83-a184-5e97-ba14-14862bec4cac.name: Man's festive ikat robe
ba3d1a83-a184-5e97-ba14-14862bec4cac.short_description: In 19th century Turkestan, an expensive Ikat coat represented wealth and dignity. Many specialists were involved in the creation of Ikat textiles, from the breeding of silk worms to the dyeing, weaving and tailoring of the cloth. Ikat silks are luxury articles. They are given as gifts at weddings and other important occasions. Ikat fabrics probably originated in China, from where they were disseminated along the network of the Silk Road throughout Central Asia.

ba4e362f-15ff-5fee-b20f-edc0e07d2d14.name: Tunic (uniform). Officer of the "Cent-Suisse" (Swiss Hundred Guard)
ba4e362f-15ff-5fee-b20f-edc0e07d2d14.description: Officer of the "Cent-Suisse" in gala uniform, carrying a pole weapon called a spontoon. The oldest Swiss Hundred Guard comprising 109 men and 4 officers was established in 1497 as a bodyguard for the French king and performed sentry duties within French royal palaces, while the Swiss Guards Regiment undertook outside duties. The "Cent-Suisse" soldiers functioned purely as guards for the royal households, and were dressed and equipped accordingly. Based on their example, the papal company of Swiss Guards was established in 1506, and it exists to this day. Other monarchs, including those of the Netherlands, Savoy, Austria, Brandenburg-Prussia, and the Electorate of Saxony, later also recruited Swiss Guards. The Swiss Hundred Guard was disbanded in 1792 during the French Revolution.

bb16c976-5f77-5e9a-b98f-840ba455f757.name: Silk sash
bb16c976-5f77-5e9a-b98f-840ba455f757.short_description: This fragment of a sash has its origins in Iran. The city of Kashan was renowned for the production of silk waist sashes. These were folded lengthways, wound around the waist and knotted at the front. Two different patterns can be seen on the same textile along the longitudinal line, so that the wearer had two sashes in one, depending on which side was turned outside. Hence the decoration was oriented on the way the object was worn. In Europe the demand for these sashes in the eighteenth century was so great that workshops were set up in Istanbul, Russia and Poland. In Poland the sashes eventually found their way into the traditional national dress of the aristocracy, which is why they are called Polish sashes (Polish: *kontusz*).

bc585e0e-7651-57e3-a5ba-853d7190ab8d.name: Fragment of an ikat- dyed cotton shawl
bc585e0e-7651-57e3-a5ba-853d7190ab8d.short_description: This inscribed fabric from Yemen is part of an ikat-dyed cotton shawl dating from the 10th century. It is a typical product of the Yemeni weaving industry with an embroidered white inscription, which quotes a passage from the Fatiha, the first chapter of the Qur’an. The *kufic* inscription displays a unified symmetry and elegance achieved by the impressive triangular endings of the letters and by a number of varied slender arch-like motifs which makes it often difficult to read.

bf855ca5-82b9-5496-8eb9-62a39c53ba92.name: Cope of signed Safavid silk fabric
bf855ca5-82b9-5496-8eb9-62a39c53ba92.short_description: The cope, an important element in the array of Christian liturgical vestments, was fashioned out of precious Iran silk. At the time, the silk manufactories of the Safavid Empire were ranked among the highest-quality production centres in the world; their products were coveted export articles. This textile presumably found its way to Europe via the trade routes and was processed after its arrival. The fact that the silk is signed indicates the how highly it was valued by those taking part in its production.

c25e83e8-79d8-5ca2-95b2-2a9dca7ab11e.description: Dating to approximately 1900, this exquisite Mekleb ornament worn on the back of the bride serves as both a significant ceremonial adornment and a powerful protective token. c2892851-42f5-54f6-a096-462c69771b8c.name: Fragment of a kaftan back
c2892851-42f5-54f6-a096-462c69771b8c.short_description: This magnificent panel from a kaftan is an example of very high-grade *seraser* production in Istanbul. *Seraser*, a material that was highly favoured at the Ottoman court, is composed of gold- and silver-wrapped silk woven in a compound structure of two warps and two or more complementary wefts. The design of peacock feathers alludes to the bird who resided in paradise until he was expelled along with Adam and Eve for failing to follow God's commandments. Eccentric largescale designs were often used on mid- to late sixteenth century textiles, as they were visible from a distance and favoured for parade garments.

c4b5ba7c-2038-5ab8-940f-807d336f261f.name: Rag costume of a Dervish
c4b5ba7c-2038-5ab8-940f-807d336f261f.short_description: Once upon a time, an individual who wanted to lead the life of a mystic and had renounced the world, donned a robe of rough wool and was identified as a Sufi, derived from the Arabic word for wool, *ṣūf*. The novice was dressed in the clothing of a dervish, the *hirqa* once admitted into a brotherhood. The tattered clothing of the Sufis expresses poverty and was stitched together from numerous patches. It is somehow also reminiscent of the colourful costume of a harlequin, with vivid lozenge-shaped stripes. It seems as if the rambling fool of God in the Commedia dell'arte slipped into the role of the half-clownish, half-demonic prankster, in order to expose the structures and mechanisms of society, attracting ridicule and disdain upon himself. Spirituality and humour can be understood as effective attempts to reveal the complex and paradox situations of which real life is so full. Nowadays a Sufi wears normal daily clothing.

c73dca1b-c179-593d-9ff2-c9e643811ee8.name: Abu Radan Dress
c73dca1b-c179-593d-9ff2-c9e643811ee8.description: Black dress with wide, open sleeves, made from cotton fabric with heavy embroidery. The chest panel shows geometrical motifs (fans) on a rose-coloured collar. The shoulders show an embroidered emblem that is known as *nishan*, and the sleeves are heavily embroidered with cypress trees and waves that include yellow braid work along the length of the sleeve. The side panels of the dress (*banayeq*) show braid work with floral motifs topped by a scissor motif (*maqas*). The lower front panel of the dress shows motifs of cypress branches in different colours. The back shows the Pasha’s tent motif bordered by geometrical figures and cypress branches, while the bottom edge of the back panel has two blue lines that go around the dress. This type of dress was used mainly for celebrations and was worn by unmarried women only for events like weddings and women-only parties. These dresses were produced by hand by the same women who wore them, thus demonstrating the female’s ability to be productive. The origins of this dress lie in Bir al-Sabe, which is one of the largest cities in Palestine and is also known as the capital of the Negev desert. Some Bir al-Sabe inhabitants are originally Bedouin tribes, which explains why the women of Bir al-Sabe used to wear these heavy dresses. The garment has the advantage of being heavy, which helps the wearer cope with the desert climate in that region; it prevents sand from entering the women’s bodies and protects them from the heat. The dress is only worn by the women of Bir al-Sabe, and it is unique to them in respect of all the colours, stitches and motifs that the dress exhibits. It is worth mentioning that while Palestinian traditional costumes are distinguished by their individuality and regionalism, they still exhibit the influence of the different stages of occupation that Palestine has witnessed throughout its long history. In this case, the Ottoman influence is reflected in the long sleeves of the dress.

cc245129-4801-5914-b91d-808b41eb1656.description: *Al-Jilaya* dress with large, open sleeves and heavy embroidery. The chest panel shows *qalayed* (necklace) embroidery and floral and geometrical motifs. The neck and shoulders are made with Ottoman striped fabric and the sleeves show patches of silk *hirmizi* fabric. The front panel of the dress has triangular shapes of silk with embroidered flowers. The *banayeq* (side panels) show rings and *Al-reesh* braid work, along with geometrical and floral motifs. The back panel has heavy and relatively long embroidery work, taking the shape of waves and geometrical figures, and is bordered with *Al-nakhl* and *Al-reesh* braid work. This is a handmade dress produced by the women of Hebron District and it is worn by married women for special occasions, especially weddings.

cc3eb98f-be74-5f38-85da-465d5c36d52e.name: Headdress
cc3eb98f-be74-5f38-85da-465d5c36d52e.short_description: A rectangular piece of Syrian silk cloth (*atlas*) with a small piece of coloured cotton cloth on the front on two sides. There is a line of Ottoman coins sewn together with three tassels dangling at the end with different stones. Silver was the most common jewellery, given by the groom to the bride as dowry. The use of Ottoman coins as pieces of jewellery – shown by women to friends and relatives – was an indirect reference to the financial status of their husbands. Silk was imported from Syria. Its trade in the Syro-Palestinian area was common because of the lack of geographical and political boundaries; some cities were like twins because of their close proximity and exchange of trade goods and business.

d04f9993-36fb-5234-ad3f-ce7d4b211668.name: Kaftan fragment.
d04f9993-36fb-5234-ad3f-ce7d4b211668.description:
A silk brocade (*kemha*) fragment that originally formed the back of a child's collarless, short-sleeved kaftan, cut with a straight waist and bell-shaped skirt. The textile is woven with a dense, overall floral design consisting of vertically disposed, sinuous floral stems with large tulips set at regular intervals. The flowers are rendered in red against a silvery green background. This type of pattern was popular not only on *kemha* fabrics, but also on other media such as tile work.  
The original museum record states that this piece represents a portion of a child's robe-of-honour from Constantinople or Bursa. Possibly arriving in Turkey via Syria, the complex weaving technique adopted on this textile, known as lampas weave, was used by Ottoman weavers in the late AH 9th–early 10th /AD late 15th–early 16th century. The most important Ottoman silk manufactory was at Bursa but in the AH 10th / AD 16th century, court workshops were also set up in Istanbul, the Ottoman capital. *Kemha* garments were designed to emphasise the imperial status of the sultan and his family even in death, when such garments were often draped over imperial cenotaphs or *sanduka*s.  
This fragment is part of a group of garments that was brought to Europe by an art dealer and cut up with some of the resulting front and back sections subsequently divided between the V&A in London and the Royal Museum in Edinburgh.
d04f9993-36fb-5234-ad3f-ce7d4b211668.short_description: This fragment comes from a child's collarless and short-sleeved silk brocade kaftan worn by a junior member of the Ottoman court. The dense, overall floral design with its vertically disposed, sinuous floral stems and large tulip heads can also be found in other media such as contemporary tile work.
d04f9993-36fb-5234-ad3f-ce7d4b211668.method_for_datation: *Kemha* textiles were popular in the Ottoman Empire between the late 10th–early 11th / late 16th–early 17th centuries.
d04f9993-36fb-5234-ad3f-ce7d4b211668.method_for_provenance: Items such as this kaftan are known to have been worked in the Ottoman silk-weaving workshops at Bursa or Istanbul during the late 10th–early 11th / late 16th–early 17th centuries.

d0e5dd9e-aee2-51d7-a5b3-d82228bcf1bd.name: Kaftan.
d0e5dd9e-aee2-51d7-a5b3-d82228bcf1bd.description:
This is an example belonging to a group known as full-length kaftans. It features hem-length decorative sleeves and slits for pockets. The fabric is brown in colour and made of threads with gilded metal wound round them by hand, a luxurious cloth known as *kemha*. The kaftan has a round collar and is woven in the form of an unfastened crossover garment; the waist is indented. It has a lower section which widens like a skirt beginning above the hips. The fabric is decorated with lotuses and peonies as well as leaves which resemble feathers; its most interesting feature is its use of a floral design with no repeat. This is frequently encountered in the textiles which belong to this group and shows that they were woven as unique examples.  
  
The *kemha* textiles are the most ostentatious in the Ottoman repertory. The cut of the kaftan is also highly careful and painstaking. The pattern is not interrupted, as can be seen in the front section and the side sections. The lining is of woven red silk with parallel lines on it. On the front of the kaftan, in the corners, the name 'Muhammad' – probably a court tailor – can be read in *kufic* script on appliqué squares. It is thought most likely that the kaftan was made for Prince Bayezid, who was killed in AH 968 / AD 1561.
d0e5dd9e-aee2-51d7-a5b3-d82228bcf1bd.short_description: Kaftans, an inseparable part of Ottoman period court life, are also the symbols of sultanate and power. This kaftan of *kemha*, a luxurious fabric, is decorated with non-repeating favourite floral motifs and is a document of the period for it bears the name of the master tailor.
d0e5dd9e-aee2-51d7-a5b3-d82228bcf1bd.dates: Second half of hegira 10th / AD 16th century.
d0e5dd9e-aee2-51d7-a5b3-d82228bcf1bd.method_for_datation: No information can be found to establish the date of this kaftan. The name 'Muhammad' appears on the front in what may be considered a maker's inscription. The maker is thought to have been a court artisan as well. Based on this information it is thought that the kaftan belonged to Prince Bayezid, who was killed in AH 968 / AD 1561.
d0e5dd9e-aee2-51d7-a5b3-d82228bcf1bd.method_for_provenance: Unknown, but Bursa was the silk and silk-textile production centre of the Ottoman Empire, and the main export centre for silk textiles such as the world-famous Ottoman brocades. It is highly likely that the textile was woven in Bursa and the kaftan was tailored at the Topkapı Palace ateliers.
d0e5dd9e-aee2-51d7-a5b3-d82228bcf1bd.obtention: The garment belonged to a resident of the palace and remains in the Topkapı Palace Museum.

d3db70b3-c132-5835-9372-de3aadb98307.short_description: This *entari* (dress) is made of turquoise satin embroidered in various stitches using silver-gilt thread. The bridal outfit is completed by a matching *hırka* (long jacket) made of the same fabric and lined with red fox fur, and matching heeled shoes with uppers of the same fabric and soles made of leather. The tailored bodice of the *entari* is lengthened by flaps of fabric that fall over the skirt, giving the *entari* the appearance of a two-piece skirt and blouse. The front of the bodice is decorated with frills. The skirt flares out from the waist downwards. The scalloped hem is trimmed with a tiny pleated frill. The jacket has a round neck and fitted sleeves, and opens down the front. The shoes are embroidered in silver and decorated at the toe with a blue-tasselled flower.

d5349934-5ade-59ea-ba16-2b2f3f97640d.name: Robe for a man
d5349934-5ade-59ea-ba16-2b2f3f97640d.short_description:
Whilst Iranian tailors customarily used local fabrics for the outside of women's and men's robes, with cheap European printed fabrics being used as linings, this man's robe (*gaba*) is the proverbial exception to this rule. The outside is made of a machine-printed cotton fabric that imitates a a very fine woollen fabric (*termeh*) from the early Qajar period. These highly esteemed fabrics were often decorated with alternating stripes in six or seven basic colours with floral patterns. Due to the presence of these stylistic similarities, it is probable that the European designers had such a fabric at their disposal when they created their design. The inner lining is made of a simply patterned Iranian fabric.  
  
This robe was acquired by the Swiss merchant Emil Alpiger in Iran between 1870 and 1896. Alpiger was then director of the Manchester-based trading company Ziegler & Co. which owned a carpet factory in Sultanabad.

d7096975-0651-52ea-8630-a12bafecd7a2.short_description: This black-blue fragment of shawl is decorated with tapestry bands woven with *kufic* inscriptions and highly stylized human figures, quadrupeds and birds. d7822972-f602-5f72-804b-41aadb287492.name: Amber/Mardan Dress
d7822972-f602-5f72-804b-41aadb287492.description: Dress made of taffeta fabric (*Al-Alam*) with chest panel in *Al-Amber* style, which is a square with geometrical shapes and floral motifs on it. The top corner of the front panel has russet velveteen trim which extends along the shoulders. The dress also has large, long sleeves with geometrical motifs embroidered on the forearm and sleeve edges. The *banayeq* (side panels) show floral motifs while the back panel shows four thick braids in the style of *Al-Qasab* needlework. The women of Beit Jala (in the Bethlehem area) embroider and sew this garment on their own, and married women wear it on a daily basis. The Bethlehem area is considered to be the centre of culture and tourism in Palestine and also has religious significance as the birthplace of Jesus. Bethlehem is famous for its traditional and religious artifacts and colourful embroidery. This dress is very distinct because it is very practical and comfortable, it guarantees ease of movement and work, and it exhibits outstanding colour.

d7bfd409-e2ad-54bc-aea9-cbf7cee1a22d.name: Bridal jewellery worn on the breasts (*Mingjuska so vot* and necklace)
d7bfd409-e2ad-54bc-aea9-cbf7cee1a22d.short_description: This piece of jewellery provides evidence on the versatility of articles of adornment worn by women in Macedonia in the 19th century. *Mingjushka so vot* belongs to the group of jewellery decorating the chests, although there is no clear distinction from pieces worn around the neck. This exquisite breast jewellery consists of a rectangular piece of broadcloth – *klashna* – covered with small silver coins reminiscent of fish scales and adorned with decorative stones. It is bordered by a chain, which is additionally adorned with coins. It used to be worn suspended on a chain. Abundant ornamentation with coins was applied on diverse pieces of jewellery and articles of adornment within all ethnic communities in Macedonia.

d951a6b1-8c1d-5dce-8a7a-81416e5bc68f.name: Kaftan fragment.
d951a6b1-8c1d-5dce-8a7a-81416e5bc68f.description:
A silk brocade (*kemha*) fragment that originally formed the back of a child's collarless, short-sleeved kaftan, cut with a straight waist and bell-shaped skirt. The textile is woven with an overall pattern of horizontal rows of dense *chintamani*, a design comprising three circles and ‘tiger-stripes’; here the circles are green and the stripes red, while the entire pattern is set against a silvery green ground.  
The *chintamani* motif is common on *kemha* textiles from about the first half of the AH 10th / AD 16th century. Its origin and meaning are still unclear, but it has been suggested that the triple-circle motif may have had apotropaic associations among Turkic peoples, warding off evil by reflecting it back at the perpetrator, while the tiger-stripes seem to recall the tiger-skin worn by the Iranian superhero Rustam.  
The original museum record states that this piece represents a portion of a child's robe-of-honour from Constantinople or Bursa. Possibly arriving in Turkey via Syria, the complex weaving technique adopted on this textile, known as lampas weave, was used by Ottoman weavers in the late AH 9th–early 10th /AD late 15th–early 16th century. The most important Ottoman silk manufactory was at Bursa but in the AH 10th / AD 16th century, court workshops were also set up in Istanbul, the Ottoman capital. *Kemha* garments were designed to emphasise the imperial status of the sultan and his family even in death, when such garments were often draped over imperial cenotaphs or *sanduka*s.
d951a6b1-8c1d-5dce-8a7a-81416e5bc68f.short_description: The *chintamani* motif on this kaftan fragment, with its triple-dot and tiger-stripe motifs, appeared on Ottoman textiles since the AH 10th / AD 16th century. Originally, the triple-dot motif may have had talismanic significance, while the tiger-stripes recall the tiger skin worn by the Iranian superhero Rustam.
d951a6b1-8c1d-5dce-8a7a-81416e5bc68f.dates: Hegira, late 10th–early 11th century / AD late 16th– early 17th century.
d951a6b1-8c1d-5dce-8a7a-81416e5bc68f.method_for_datation: *Kemha* textiles were popular in the Ottoman Empire between the late 10th–early 11th / late 16th–early 17th centuries.
d951a6b1-8c1d-5dce-8a7a-81416e5bc68f.method_for_provenance: Items such as this kaftan are known to have been worked in the Ottoman silk-weaving workshops at Bursa or Istanbul during the late 10th–early 11th / late 16th–early 17th centuries.

dbf4dc13-3f6b-5da9-bf05-cfabe7876ad3.name: Headdress
dbf4dc13-3f6b-5da9-bf05-cfabe7876ad3.short_description: A silver circular disk with inherent decorations in the carving, and prominent dome above; chains dangling with oval shapes at the end. With two different length. This ornament was placed on the top of a high hat worn by al-Druze (Druse) women. Silver was the most common jewellery. The dowry of silver and gold jewellery was given by the groom to the bride, reflecting the financial status of the groom. This object illustrates the variegated social composition and the demographic changes in the Jordanian territory in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The al-Druze tribes migrated from Syria (Hawran) to north east Jordan in the early twentieth century because of their support for the Syrian revolution against the French occupation.

dc620fad-84b0-5474-b1ee-8a583440c84a.name: Textile fragment from Archbishop Ximenez de Rada's burial garments
dc620fad-84b0-5474-b1ee-8a583440c84a.description: The textile fragment was part of the alb which was buried the Archbishop Rodrigo Ximénez de Rada in 1247 at the Monastery of Santa María de Huerta (Soria, Spain). The tomb was opened at the beginning of the decade of 1880 at the request of the Master of Sigüenza. The fragment was found in the coffin and the master give it to the Marquis of Cerralbo, who was present. After this event, because of the importance of the Archbishop garments and the marquis’ interest in the history of the Monastery, the marquis paid all the expenses of two new openings of the grave. The first one in 1886 for the Spanish Royal Academy of the History researches, and the second one in 1907 for his own studio, when he completed the description of the garments and took photographs to his publication in 1908.

dd51c631-efa7-5621-9c17-104499a84fde.name: Textile fragment from a dalmatic of the so called *Heinrichsgewänder* (vestments) in the Alte Kapelle chapel in Regensburg
dd51c631-efa7-5621-9c17-104499a84fde.short_description: This fragment came into the MAK textile collection through a purchase of textiles negotiated by the Aachen Canon Franz Bock in 1865. Beforehand, it was part of the so called *Heinrichsgewänder* (vestments) in the Alte Kapelle chapel in Regensburg. ddd75581-2e37-5baa-8483-63c54f368af5.name: Dress
ddd75581-2e37-5baa-8483-63c54f368af5.short_description: Long black silk dress (*malas*), narrow at the waist, wide at the bottom, embroidered with cross-stitch dark blue and red on the chest and on the front side, worn by women of the al-Druze tribes, with a shirt underneath. This object illustrates the variegated composition and the demographic changes of the Jordan population in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It also shows how the different populations brought with them their fashion, costumes and rites which contributed to the multifaceted social and cultural heritage of Jordan. The al-Druze tribes migrated from Syria (Hawran) to northeast Jordan in the early twentieth century because of their support for the Syrian revolution against the French occupation.

dec4ca65-fe43-5a16-8c53-e4d5c9648ac8.short_description: The kaftan is cut with straight flaring skirts and has short sleeves that have been repaired with a later fabric. The loom width of the crimson silk fabric is woven with four undulating vertical stems which bear round stylized pomegranates and small rosettes. dfd2eeea-301b-506a-85f9-f9ad927ce8f2.name: Dress
dfd2eeea-301b-506a-85f9-f9ad927ce8f2.short_description: Women's costumes of the central regions of Jordan are characterized by length, dark colours, light vertical strips of embroidery and very long sleeves. This black and blue dress has a very loose fitting, open chest and long flared sleeves pulled over a head band. The length of the dress was adjusted to the height of the woman by a sash. Wide at the bottom, it is decorated horizontally with blue cotton stripes and vertically with embroidery lines and Ottoman coins. The traditional costumes reflect the variegated population composition and demographic changes of the late 19th century-early 20th century Jordanian territory, when new waves of people arrived and settled for the purpose of trades and crafts. Craft was not limited to the everyday life and the profits from crafts were a source of income.

e160d8e8-b92a-510d-9233-09013a954962.name: Kaftan.
e160d8e8-b92a-510d-9233-09013a954962.description: The front half of a child's kaftan, woven of white, blue, and gold on a red satin ground (the back half was transferred to the National Museum of Scotland in the 19th century). The decorative pattern is a repeated wavy line which is thought to be based on the tiger-skin armour of the legendary Iranian hero, Rustam. Similar motifs can be seen on many Ottoman artworks of the 16th century and later (see for example, the 18th-century chimneypiece also at the Victoria and Albert Museum). Kaftans like this would have been worn by children at the Ottoman court, both princes and pages. The horizontal bands, or frogging, are thought to have indicated the wearer's rank. When the owner died, some of his state dress, such as kaftans, would be draped over his cenotaph, and then in turn carpets and other textiles were draped over it and periodically added or replaced. This practice had the beneficial result of preserving the original clothing for a remarkably long time; a garment belonging to Sultan Selim I (d. AH 926 / AD 1520) was said to have been present on top of his tomb as recently as the mid-20th century.
e160d8e8-b92a-510d-9233-09013a954962.short_description: The front half of a child’s kaftan, woven in white, blue and gold on a red satin ground. Kaftans like this would have been worn by children at the Ottoman court, both princes and pages. When the owner died the kaftan was placed atop his tomb.
e160d8e8-b92a-510d-9233-09013a954962.method_for_datation: Part of a group of kaftans said to have come from Ottoman tombs dating to the 16th century; the design is consistent with clothing from that period as known from other garments and as seen in Ottoman miniature painting.

e179ff65-79d3-5bba-97ab-c8056af7e861.name: Handkerchief/ textile fragment.
e179ff65-79d3-5bba-97ab-c8056af7e861.description:
A handkerchief square, bordered along two of its sides by a series of silk-embroidered bands of chain stitch in red, yellow, black and white. Each series of bands is composed of an outer band, embellished by two undulating branches, flanking smaller ones. Next to this decorative band, is a broader one that is composed in its turn, of three smaller bands: The two border bands are decorated with a repetitive inscription in *kufic* script of the owner's name: 'al-bi-Allah'. The middle band is embellished by a successive series of birds with flying leaves drifting from their necks; this band is flanked by two thin borders filled with geometric decorative motifs.  
This handkerchief is attributed to the Fatimid caliph, al-'Aziz bi-Allah who ruled from AH 365–86 / AD 975–96, and who was known for his tolerant policies towards the Copts, and his patronage and encouragement of the craftsmen of the Coptic community to the point where they exerted great efforts to excel in their arts and craftsmanship. The artisans used decorative components that were influenced to a large extent by Coptic art, such as for instance the portrayal of pigeons inside roundels.  
Various types of textile production flourished during the Fatimid period, and silk was used extensively in the decoration and embellishment of textiles. The Fatimid Empire enjoyed great wealth, and this was reflected in splendid appearances in various aspects of their lives, and in particular in their apparel, which included richly woven and embroidered turbans, cloaks and handkerchiefs.
e179ff65-79d3-5bba-97ab-c8056af7e861.short_description: Fatimid caliphs paid great attention to the textile industry and appointed a master of *Tiraz* to supervise textile affairs. Some silk textiles were made only for the caliph, including this piece, which bears the name of the Fatimid Caliph al-'Aziz bi-Allah in embroidery.
e179ff65-79d3-5bba-97ab-c8056af7e861.method_for_datation: This piece was dated based on the band of inscription, which consists of the name of the Fatimid caliph, al-'Aziz bi-Allah (r. 365–86 / 975–96).
e179ff65-79d3-5bba-97ab-c8056af7e861.method_for_provenance: This handkerchief is attributed to the Fatimid caliph, al-'Aziz bi-Allah who ruled in Egypt from AH 365–86 / AD 975–96.

e3f48d7b-3bf0-5b73-ae59-24ec80351340.short_description: The Tantur is an example of cultural tradition developed inside the contaminations typical of the Mediterranean world. It is decorated with symbolic images of leaves, flowers and animals and it is engraved with the year of Egira, 1172. Its cylindrical shape is reminiscent of an *asherah*, one of the emblems of the Phoenician goddess of fertility Astarte (the Siriac Atargotis), often represented with cylindrical headgear. The origins in terms of scientific activity and conservation of Museo Nazionale Preistorico Etnografico "Luigi Pigorini" in Rome, can be traced back to the foundation in 1875 of the "Royal National Museum of Prehistory and Ethnography in Rome" within the buildings of the Roman College.

e4d13bf7-94a1-5333-82e7-c8fa33d3b864.name: Robe
e4d13bf7-94a1-5333-82e7-c8fa33d3b864.short_description: The cut of this male garment is typically Mongol with its full skirt for riding, its broad wrap-over, the extremely long sleeves and waist support made of silk cords. The textile itself worked with metal threads has a design with small medallions enclosing the images of *djeiran*, lion and lotus. Such garments made of cloth of gold were worn by the highest ranks of Mongol society. Nomads of Central Asia treasured textiles and used them to convey status.

e5df4439-6b33-58df-9ad0-3342565ff30f.name: Horsetail
e5df4439-6b33-58df-9ad0-3342565ff30f.short_description: Tulgars with horse tails were ancient Ottoman symbols denoting social rank; the Turks had brought them with them when they emigrated from their Central-Asian homeland. Part of Archduke Ferdinand’s Turkish booty, this one may have been used during his “Hussars’ tournaments”. The shape and number of horse tails denoted the rank of an Ottoman dignitary. They were placed in front of his tent and accompanied him when the army was on the march. The Sultan was accorded seven or even nine horse tails as a symbol of his authority.

e733f2a6-8940-5e1d-ba96-bb338e5c87f6.name: Hooded cloak (*burnus*)
e733f2a6-8940-5e1d-ba96-bb338e5c87f6.description: Cloak in green velvet with stencilled decoration of pomegranates and leaves in brown. This velvet is based on the Venetian ones of the 15th and 16th centuries. The cloak has a wide fullness at the bottom and a big hood, formed by four points. The cloak is lined in a green silk, printed in silver vegetal motifs.

e7789911-13d5-5689-9f57-6f31db64cdef.name: Jillayeh Wedding Dress
e7789911-13d5-5689-9f57-6f31db64cdef.description: Black dress with heavy embroidery. The chest panel shows chevron pattern embroidery, which is also known as *qalayed* (necklace), as well as many floral motifs, while the back panel shows floral motifs embroidered on silk fabric with special stitches. The sleeves are heavily embroidered with vine leaves, while the *banayeq* (side panels) show motifs of flowers, feathers and *manajel* (thick braid work connecting the dress parts). This dress is mainly worn by the married women of Hebron for ceremonial events like weddings. Located in the West Bank, south of Jerusalem, and founded by the Canaanites in the early Bronze Age, Hebron has been famous since ancient times for handicrafts, including ceramics, pottery, glass, embroidery and leather. This gown is handmade from silk and cashmere using atlas stitch. The dress is worn only by married women of Hebron, and it is unique to them in respect of all the colours, stitches, floral motifs and vine leaf motifs that the dress exhibits. The bottom front panel has yellow, orange and red silk triangles with Kashmir cloth on the sides. The bottom of the back panel has a stitched-in piece of cloth with blue embroidered birds and flowers. The use of birds and flowers does not bear any hidden symbolism; rather, it reflects the continuous work of women on the land and hence their use of nature as a main source of inspiration for their embroidery, not only in Hebron but other regions of Palestine as well.

e8eaafdf-a77c-51a2-8c54-e52092c06b0b.name: Calligraphic *Limar* Cloth
e8eaafdf-a77c-51a2-8c54-e52092c06b0b.short_description:
Silk *limar* cloth; predominantly blue & red. White calligraphic pattern on blue ground on the central compartment & stylised motif of bamboo shoots (*pucuk rebung*) & geometric patterns on red ground (*punca kain*) at each end of the *sarong*. Identifiable words: '*La Ilaha Il Allah*' - There is no God but Allah & *Muhammadur Rasul* (Allah) - Prophet Muhammad is His Messenger. Calligraphic pattern suggests it was not worn as a garment. Perhaps utilised in ceremonial practice such as coffin cover etc.  
  
Click [here](< https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QRi5sCkwpgY>) to **watch a video presentation** of this artefact.

e8fc4581-ee8f-583c-a11e-54b1e44bda1a.short_description: Padded bag to hold three small brass bottles of Arab eye-liner, perfumes and essential oils. It was used as a wall decoration. Decorated with silk tassels, glass beads, Egyptian and Ottoman coins. The Jordanian economy relied on trades and crafts and new waves of people started to settle in the Jordanian territory for these purposes. This object is an example of how traditional fashion reflected the variegated population composition of the area in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It is also an example of local personal attire, fashion, costumes and rites.

e96b2d33-110e-54cc-b032-89470c72fd09.name: Head- and shoulder shawl
e96b2d33-110e-54cc-b032-89470c72fd09.short_description:
The *bakhnūg* is a rectangular woollen head-scarf worn by women. It is soberly decorated (two or three narrow lines along the border, a small piece of individual embroidery in one corner, a fish, a star, a line) or with large planes of linear or geometrical designs woven into the fabric (straight, diagonal or zig-zag lines, dots, angles, triangles or a rhombus ­with endless possibilities of combinations).  
A *bakhnūg* was made at home by its future wearer for her personal use and this could take up to two or three years to create: preparation of the wool, spinning, setting up the vertical loom, weaving, as well as incorporating the designs of white cotton thread on a white wool background. When completed, the *bakhnūg* was left white (for a young girl), dyed carmine (for a bride or newly-married women), indigo or black (for older women); when dyed, only the woollen background changes colour, setting off the filigree designs of the cotton embroidery.

e99ae084-468e-510d-90bc-109658d66887.description: Example of sarma, an Ottoman metallic-thread embroidery technique, spread across the Levant during Ottoman rule as urban communities adopted and embraced the style as part of elite and festive dress. Characterised by intricate gold and silver threadwork, sarma became particularly associated with urban centres such as Jerusalem, Jaffa, and Damascus, where members of the social elite wore richly embellished garments on ceremonial and festive occasions.

eb0069e6-ef9d-5223-afab-ebd48196c101.name: Sab’aawi Dress
eb0069e6-ef9d-5223-afab-ebd48196c101.description: Black dress with wide, long sleeves and *aqras* (geometrical figures) embroidered on the chest panel. The shoulders and upper sleeves show geometrical figures with cypress tree braid work. The sleeve opening has a *tashreefa* motif with white and red colours. The front panel and the *banayeq* (side panels) have heavy cypress tree motif embroidery, while the back panel shows an atlas motif with moons and geometrical figures. The top shows cypress tree designs and the bottom edge of the dress shows two lines of blue embroidery. This handmade dress originally comes from the Bir al-Sabe district. It is an everyday dress, and all women can wear it day to night. It is casual and comfortable, allowing them to do their house chores easily, and is also very practical and easy to wear.

ecda8323-4cc5-5e96-a034-122e8ca1bb6c.name: Textile from the Prince Felipe of Castile burial
ecda8323-4cc5-5e96-a034-122e8ca1bb6c.description: This fragment came from the set of garments wore by the Castilian Prince Phillip in his burial at Villalcázar de Sirga (Palencia). ed9865de-73ac-57f6-ade6-ad41f83cd57d.name: Section from a chasuble with ogival medallions
ed9865de-73ac-57f6-ade6-ad41f83cd57d.short_description:
The fabric is of very high-quality weave, and is datable on the basis of its technique and design to the early years of the classical era of Ottoman silk lampas (*kemha*) in the 1550s, when the designers and weavers, encouraged by state patronage at the very highest level, were establishing themselves in competition with Italian silk weavers. The tiny scale of the stylized blossoms, the precision of their drawing and their symmetrical arrangement are all indications of a fairly early date.  
Fabrics of this sort, exported to western and central Europe, were frequently fashioned into ecclesiastical vestments, the chasuble being the most common genre to incorporate both Ottoman *kemha* and Ottoman velvet.  
The two halves of the other side of this chasuble are in the Textile Museum, Washington, DC, inv. no.1.51; and the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, inv. no.08.109.24.

effaa1df-9ca1-5f7e-bc65-9a7edb7a597c.name: Tunic (uniform). Officer in the regiment of Swiss Guards, quartermaster general in Holland.
effaa1df-9ca1-5f7e-bc65-9a7edb7a597c.description: Uniform of Albert Dietegen von Planta from Zuoz (b. 1740, d. March or May 1803), major general and inspector of the Dutch infantry. In 1795, von Planta returned to Switzerland where he acted as deputy to the war council of the Three Leagues (Canton of Grisons). Between 1568 and 1829, a total of 80,000 Swiss troops is estimated to have fought for the Dutch on thirty-one occasions. In 1672, King William III (William of Orange) took into service some 100 Swiss halberdiers as his personal bodyguard, the so-called "Guardes Zwitzers". In the second half of the eighteenth century, Holland had a regiment of Swiss Guards and several Swiss line regiments, largely comprising men from the Protestant canton of Bern, but also from Zurich and Grisons; they were disbanded in 1796. The last four Swiss regiments served in Holland from 1814 until their disbandment in 1829.

f0667100-6159-569b-9a0e-84fec1b968f0.name: Headdress
f0667100-6159-569b-9a0e-84fec1b968f0.short_description: Three bands of silver chain fitted around the sides and over the crown of the head and attached to a surrounding fabric patterned in minute beadwork and sewn with various Ottoman and Russian coins. From this head-piece hangs a long piece of cotton sewn with coins of the Ottoman Empire with a rectangular pendant and multiple red and green silk tassels on the back. Headdresses like this one were worn by married women, as silver was the most common jewellery. The dowry of silver and gold jewellery was given by the groom to the bride. The Ottoman and Russian coins reflect the social and economic situation of Jordan between the end of the 19th century and the early 20th century, when it was part of the Ottoman empire and it was influenced by population movements, demographic changes and trade with distant countries.

f29b84af-a354-519f-abf4-763d9a15df5a.name: White Rumi Dress
f29b84af-a354-519f-abf4-763d9a15df5a.description: Dress made of white, handwoven raw linen, embroidered mostly with red and pink silk. The embroidery is cross-stitch in traditional Ramallah motif and colour pattern. The dress comes with basic long sleeves that show floral motifs under the arms and on the cuffs. Two identical, thick embroidery stripes sit on each side of the waist, with heavy embroidery on the border. One of the most distinguishing features of this dress is the shape of the *qabbeh* (chest panel) and the chevron on it. The chest panel is embroidered with different motifs. The centre of the panel has a chevron topped by two branches of flowers and, under it, two squares of embroidery with feathers on the sides. The panel is framed by flowers and a few feather motifs embroidered on the edges. This dress is considered to be the traditional wedding dress in Ramallah. It is very distinctive because Ramallah is one of few regions that uses white fabric and, even here, white is relatively rare. Some women might also wear this style of dress, but with different stitches, on a daily basis, and this is what makes the Ramallah dress so special. Ramallah is a Palestinian city in the central West Bank, north of Jerusalem, and is generally considered the most affluent and cultural, as well as the most liberal, of all Palestinian cities. Like most Palestinian areas, Ramallah has a rich culture of song, dance and costumes. We see examples of Palestinian attire in artifacts from the Canaanite period. Before the Palestinian Nakba in the 1948 war, traditional costumes for Palestinian women varied regionally in design.

f310be0c-2e4a-5a7a-ab0c-baaa41091e32.name: *Dokhla* (wedding dress)
f310be0c-2e4a-5a7a-ab0c-baaa41091e32.short_description: This tunic is entirely embroidered with gold-plated silver thread. This is the most important element of the marriage ceremony (jelwa) in Nabeul (Tunisia). The rectangular tunic's splendour comes from its incredibly rich embroidery, which is made of various different silk ribbons, all embellished with tal. In fact, the embroidery entirely covers the fabric itself. The breast and belt areas are embroidered with sequins and gold thread. The tunic is calf-length, and a luxurious pair of silk trousers can be seen beneath, covered in gold embroidery to match the sleeves. In addition to this, one of the bride's many items of jewellery is a great chain of golden rings, a rihana, which she wears with a large necklace made of a scented material. Lastly, the bride's head is covered by an embroidered veil made of muslin and silk.

keywords: Embroidery from Nabeul; sequins and gold thread

f9788b95-591f-522c-bd57-84003553fdd9.name: *Üçetek entari*
f9788b95-591f-522c-bd57-84003553fdd9.short_description: The attire of Ottoman women included dresses for the outdoors and the indoors. Starting from early 19th century, dresses called *üçetek* (dress with three skirts) and *dörtetek* (dress with four skirts) became fashionable. As relations with Europe increased, women in Istanbul started to use imported European textiles for their new dresses. This *üçetek entari* (dress with three skirts) is made of a soft red-coloured *canfes* (fine-textured shiny silk fabric) embroidered in the laid cord technique. The robe has a long trailing skirt, wrist-length sleeves and a stand-up collar. It fastens across the chest with button loops and plaited buttons. Along the edges of the skirt, sleeves, slits and seams are undulating floral designs embroidered in coloured silk cord.
f9788b95-591f-522c-bd57-84003553fdd9.holder: Vehbi Koç Foundation Sadberk Hanim Museum
keywords: fashion; traditional dress; textile

f9a18ff2-f597-5b8b-bbfe-3e66d75ad509.name: Beit Dajan Wedding Dress
f9a18ff2-f597-5b8b-bbfe-3e66d75ad509.description: Black dress made of black linen fabric. The chest panel of the dress is framed on three sides with different colours, surrounding a *tashreefa* motif. It has a V-neck collar with tassels, and is embellished with lulu braid work that has flowers on both ends. The neck and shoulders are made of wine-coloured linen fabric with a thick orange lacing. The sleeves include *hirmizi* fabric with multiple colours of embroidery and framed by lulu braid work with flowers. The back panel of the dress shows flowers on two sides with an oval in the centre. The *banayeq* (side panels) include soft floral motifs with geometrical shapes, surrounded by trim in geometrical motifs. A lulu braid work with flowers is seen on the centre of the front panel, while the back shows horizontal braid work of cypress trees and vertical braid work similar to the front panel. This dress is representative of garments from Beit Dajan, a Palestinian village located to the east of Nablus. Beit Dajan is famous for its fertile agricultural land, which may be a great source of inspiration for the embroidery on this garment. The women of Beit Dajan village embroider and sew this type of garment on their own, and they wear it on occasions and celebrations like weddings. It is not suitable for daily life as it is heavy and ornate.

f9ae9656-29ab-534b-a02c-90fe95d65205.name: Three pairs of clogs
f9ae9656-29ab-534b-a02c-90fe95d65205.short_description: Wooden clogs such as these have a long history in the Middle East, emerging before the Middle Ages and remaining popular for centuries to come. They were made of a variety of woods, including walnut, apricot, willow, poplar, or beech. The wood was cut into wedge shapes then moulded around the foot of the wearer. Excess wood was then shaved off, the heel attached, and the wood painted and polished. Leather girdles in a variety of colours were fixed to the heel with special nails and the wood would often be decorated with mosaics of bone or seashells organised in geometric or floral patterns. These shoes were designed to be comfortable and resistant to water, and thus were usually worn at home, particularly by women.

keywords: Shoes; Woodwork; Fashion

f9c5a022-ba1e-5b5b-a490-3b54263c0271.name: *Daffah khachyya*
f9c5a022-ba1e-5b5b-a490-3b54263c0271.short_description: This was purchased from Sheikh Sa\`ud’s family collection in 2001. The cloak is handmade and hand embroidered, made from heavy black wool. It is estimated to be older than 1960, between the 1940’s and the 1950’s. It is speculated that it was used by the Bedouins from eastern Saudi Arabia. It is called *daffah khachyya* and not *bisht*. *Khachyya* is the man who would have been involved in making the cloaks.

fab32475-cc0b-58fd-b8a1-2d333ca79a85.name: Silk garment.
fab32475-cc0b-58fd-b8a1-2d333ca79a85.description:
An exquisite garment made of silk and finely woven with great skill. It is in excellent condition and it is likely that the owner of the garment wore it for official receptions and ceremonies. The garment is made up of two pieces: the inner piece and the outer piece. The inner garment is a silk robe, soft to the touch, in yellow. It has a simple design that resembles a *disdasha / jalabiya* (a long, loose flowing garment). This garment has an open collar to the waist, but a large section of the opening is brought together with bands of fabric that can be opened and then closed in a different place.  
The outer garment is a loose flowing gown, which is open in front along its length and resembles an *'aba'a* \[robe\] which covers the body completely and allows freedom of movement. This garment is made from skilfully woven, soft silk of blue and white bestowing on the wearer stature and elegance. The outer robe is embroidered in the same shade of yellow as the inner garment.  
The embroidery is centred on the edges of the opening of the robe, and covers most of both sleeves; it includes blossoms and vegetal stems which are executed with thick silk thread.  
This garment is a good example of fashionable clothing for women of the upper classes in Ottoman society of the 13th / 19th century, showing also individual selectivity and fine taste in the choice of fabric and colours.
fab32475-cc0b-58fd-b8a1-2d333ca79a85.short_description: A silk garment intricately woven with great skill. It is in good condition and was probably worn for official occasions. It consists of an inner soft silk yellow garment and an outer robe-like garment that covers the body completely. It is open in the front along its length and is made of blue and white soft silk imparting stature and elegance to the wearer.
fab32475-cc0b-58fd-b8a1-2d333ca79a85.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
fab32475-cc0b-58fd-b8a1-2d333ca79a85.initial_owner: The wife of Ya’qub Pasha, governor of Jerusalem AH 1245 / AD 1830.
fab32475-cc0b-58fd-b8a1-2d333ca79a85.method_for_datation: The piece was dated based on the date in which Ya'qub Pasha (husband of the owner of the garment) governed Jerusalem.
fab32475-cc0b-58fd-b8a1-2d333ca79a85.method_for_provenance: This type of silken textile was famous all over Turkey especially in Istanbul, and also in Syria. Besides this information there is no means of ascertaining in which of the two countries it was made, or whether it was somewhere else entirely.
fab32475-cc0b-58fd-b8a1-2d333ca79a85.provenance: Possibly produced in either Syria or Turkey.

fbf4d4a8-5487-5f14-80a9-c326b47bc923.name: Kaftan fragment.
fbf4d4a8-5487-5f14-80a9-c326b47bc923.description:
A silk brocade (*kemha*) fragment that originally formed the back of a child's collarless, short-sleeved kaftan, cut with a straight waist and bell-shaped skirt. The textile is woven with staggered rows of diagonally ascending zigzag bands set at regular intervals, in red, which are further enhanced by a pattern, in miniature, of ‘tiger stripes’ and three circles (known as *chintamani*), rendered in green. The *chintamani* motif is common on *kemha* textiles from about the first half of the AH 10th / AD 16th century. Its origin and meaning are still unclear, but it has been suggested that the triple-circle motif may have had apotropaic associations among Turkic peoples, warding off evil by reflecting it back at the perpetrator, while the tiger-stripes seem to recall the tiger-skin worn by the Iranian superhero Rustam.  
The original museum record states that this piece represents a portion of a child's robe-of-honour from Constantinople or Bursa. Possibly arriving in Turkey via Syria, the complex weaving technique adopted on this textile, known as lampas weave, was used by Ottoman weavers in the late AH 9th–early 10th /AD late 15th–early 16th century. The most important Ottoman silk manufactory was at Bursa but in the AH 10th / AD 16th century, court workshops were also set up in Istanbul, the Ottoman capital. *Kemha* garments were designed to emphasise the imperial status of the sultan and his family even in death, when such garments were often draped over imperial cenotaphs or *sanduka*s.  
This fragment is part of a group of garments that was brought to Europe by an art dealer and cut up with some of the resulting front and back sections subsequently divided between the V&A in London and the Royal Museum in Edinburgh.
